S1 · Traffic

Social Media Content

Cut one pillar into clips, 60-second videos and quotes, batch them and post every 3 days.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Turn one pillar piece into a week-by-week batch of social posts, without writing anything from scratch. You'll cut the pillar into five clips, trim the best into 60-second videos, pull quotes and graphics, batch everything in your content calendar, tag every link and schedule a post every 3 days. You're done when the batch is scheduled before the week starts and every link carries utm_source=social.

Steps
8
Examples
7
Runs On
GA4 · Canva · Metricool · LinkedIn · Beehiiv

How This Changes by Mechanism

Posts are dated and point at registration. Post to the event every 3 days and refresh the date before the next cycle.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Start From One Pillar

    Your pillar is the blog post from the Blog guide, or the recording of a session. Everything else is cut from it. Batch, never improvise: writing posts one at a time on the day is how the channel quietly stops.

    Capture Needed

    A pillar blog post or session recording open next to the content calendar page that lists what will be cut from it.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Cut Five Clips

    Cut the five best moments from the pillar, 2–4 minutes each. Pick the bits that answer a real objection or show the method working.

    Post them first, then note which ones people engaged with most. Those are what the next round is cut from.

    Capture Needed

    A video editor timeline with five clip ranges marked on one recording.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Trim the Winners to 60 Seconds

    Take the clips that landed and trim each to a 60-second video. This round usually drives the most traffic, so don't skip it to save time.

    Add captions, so the clip still works with the sound off.

    Capture Needed

    A 60-second vertical clip being exported with captions on.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Pull Quotes and Graphics

    From what resonated, lift single lines word for word and turn them into quote cards, a simple graphic or a poll. A tool like Canva works; keep one template so every card looks like yours.

    Capture Needed

    Canva editor with a quote-card template and an anonymised quote.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Batch Everything in Your Calendar

    Put every clip, video and quote into your Notion content calendar, one card per post, with its date and platform. Plan a post about your event every 3 days until the session.

  6. 6
    Tag Every Link

    Every post that links to your page carries a UTM. Build it in Google's Campaign URL Builder ↗: source social (or the platform name), medium organic, campaign {event_slug}_{date}.

    Without the tag, none of this can be traced to a registration.

  7. 7
    Schedule the Batch

    Load the batch into Metricool (or your scheduler) and set the dates. Scheduling isn't sending: nothing goes live until the scheduled time, so you can still edit.

    Once a post goes live it's public. Read it once more in the scheduler's preview before the week starts.

    Capture Needed

    Metricool planner calendar with scheduled posts across a week (Metricool help centre).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  8. 8
    Read Clicks, Not Likes

    Each week, check clicks to your registration page in Google Analytics, filtered to source social. Likes and comments aren't traffic.

    The clips and quotes that drove clicks decide what you cut from the next pillar. Your best-performing topics also feed the 52-week newsletter rotation.

Green dashboard. Wrong numbers. Both true at the same time. That is the state most Data Estates are in, and nobody finds out until a business user says

“Hmmm …the report looks off?” Here is how it happens.

A new source gets added and somebody wires up a Health check that asks one question:

“Did the pipeline complete?”

Nobody instruments the quality. The pipeline runs. The data arrives.

…Nobody knows whether it is right. Now apply the same blind spot to your Databricks Bill. That Health Check never asks “What the run cost is?”

So a job doing two minutes of real work sits inside a cluster that takes 10 minutes to spin up and 10 to spin down.

FACT: In some environments, 60-75 of every 100 minutes you are billed for is startup and shutdown rather than work. Every one of those runs reports success. Alongside that, data gets appended daily and never compacted or compressed, so storage and processing quietly cost more every month for the same result. Neither gap is worth stopping for on its own. That is exactly why they accumulate. Months later the un-monitored surface of your estate is enormous, and your bill has been funding it the whole time. None of this needs a rebuild.

Cost spikes keep returning. The cycle must be eliminated, not patched Most Databricks cost work is done as a project. Somebody audits the estate, finds the waste, right-sizes the obvious things, and the next invoice drops. Everybody is pleased. Then the programme ends, the team returns to delivery, and two quarters later the number is back. Without visibility into workload costs, the same billing surprises occur every quarter. Engineering teams spend more time explaining costs than delivering value. This is the third of the three business problems, and it is the one that decides whether the other two stay solved. Shock billing you can survive. Blocked innovation you can escalate. Operational chaos that keeps recurring is the one that quietly tells your finance team that data cost is simply unmanageable, and that assumption is expensive for years. Cutover is a moment. Monitoring is how you keep the promise you made. Four things need watching continuously after any optimisation or migration, not quarterly:

  • Cost. Are we better than baseline? DBU and cloud spend, idle clusters, failed-run waste, cost per pipeline
  • Performance. Are SLAs holding? Duration at p95, queue time, throughput, data freshness
  • Data correctness. Is output still trusted? Dual-run diffs, reconciliation, data quality checks, anomaly alerts
  • Governance. Is the platform healthy? Catalog coverage, policy violations, secrets and access, compliance That is the migration control tower, and it runs on a loop: detect, act, improve, optimise, re-assess. Alerts and anomalies get caught, workloads get right-sized and remediated, pipelines get optimised, the baseline gets updated, and the next wave gets planned from the new number rather than the old one. Prove value and catch drift before your users do. A saving you cannot prove is a saving finance will not credit you with next year. And a baseline nobody is watching is not a baseline. It is a screenshot from the quarter you finished the project. Every month without this, the estate drifts back toward the number you already paid to fix. We are walking through the control tower and the full Assessment, Migration, Monitor framework on the masterclass. Register before the next quarter undoes the last one. Link in the first comment.

You Are Reprocessing Five Years Of History Every Night To Add One Day

Somewhere in your Databricks estate there is a job that reads five years of history every night so that it can add one day to the end of it. It is not broken. That is exactly why nobody has found it. Full refresh is how almost every pipeline starts. It is simpler to write, it is easier to reason about, and when the table was small it cost close to nothing. Then the table grew. The job kept doing precisely what it was told, and the cost of that instruction grew with it, every night, for years. No alert fires. The job succeeds. The data is correct. The only symptom is a runtime that has been creeping up for so long that whatever it is now feels normal. And it compounds in the worst possible direction. The more successful your data platform is, the more history you accumulate, and the more you pay each night to reprocess history that has not changed since the day it landed. This is one of the most concentrated single-job costs I find in any estate, and it is almost always in a pipeline nobody has opened in two years. The fix is not exotic and it is not a re-architecture. It is the difference between "rebuild the table" and "add what is new". Usually that means a watermark, a merge, and a change to how the job decides what it actually needs to read. How to spot it, and the four changes that fix it, are in the carousel.

Maya Okonkwopost 1

"Our controls are broadly sound" is no longer an available answer.

Provision 29 of the UK Corporate Governance Code applies to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2026.

Boards must now declare, in the annual report, whether their material controls were effective at the balance sheet date.

Not improving. Not adequate. Effective.

And the board decides what counts as material.

Three things that changes:

1. Material controls are not only financial controls, they extend to operational, reporting and compliance controls, which is exactly where most regulated firms are thinnest.
2. The declaration is an outcome rather than a process, so a description of your assurance framework no longer substitutes for a view on whether the thing actually worked.
3. The FRC revised three audit standards in June 2026 to cover auditor responsibilities for the Provision 29 statement, which means your declaration will be read by someone with a professional duty to notice inconsistency.

For December year ends, the first statements land in early 2027.

The evidence trail for them is being built now, in this year's board papers.

Some directors will sign having asked for the control map and the list of exceptions.

Others will sign having read a summary.

Only one of those positions is defensible.

I cover the personal exposure side of this in our free masterclass, The Insider Roadmap to Access Top UK Fintech Board Seats in 2026.

S1 · Traffic

Paid Ads

Track the registration first, then test two ads on the smallest budget and scale only what converts.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Buy traffic only after you can see what it buys. You'll mark the registration as the conversion in your analytics and ad accounts, start a retargeting pool on day one, launch two ads that differ only in angle on the smallest budget, and judge them weekly by cost per lead. You're done when a test registration shows up as a conversion in both Meta and Google, and both ads are live with tagged links.

Steps
9
Examples
7
Runs On
GA4 · Meta Ads · Google Ads

How This Changes by Mechanism

Ads run in a dated window before the session and switch off after it. The retargeting pool carries over to the next date.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Make the Registration Your Conversion

    A conversion is the action you pay to get. Here it's the registration form being submitted, not a page view.

    Before spending anything, check that your registration page and thank-you page send their events to Google Analytics. An ad account tracking an unmeasured page just spends money blind.

    Capture Needed

    GA4 → Admin → Events (or Key events) with the registration event marked as a key event.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Install the Meta Pixel

    The pixel is a small snippet that tells Meta when someone visits or registers.

    1. In Meta Events Manager, click Connect data → Web and create a pixel.
    2. Enter your registration page address and follow the setup it offers.
    3. Map the registration to Meta's Lead or CompleteRegistration event.
    4. Open Test events, load your page and check the visit shows up.
    Capture Needed

    Meta Events Manager → Connect data → Web → Create pixel dialog (owner session; Meta's help pages carry no screenshot).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Add the Google Conversion
    1. In Google Ads, open Goals → Conversions → New conversion action → Website.
    2. Add the Google tag to your site, or connect it through Google Tag Manager.
    3. Set the registration as a primary conversion, so bidding optimises for it.
  4. 4
    Start the Retargeting Pool on Day One

    A retargeting pool is everyone who visited your page but didn't register. It needs time to fill, so create it before any ad runs.

    In Meta, open Audiences → Create audience → Custom audience → Website, pick your pixel and choose all website visitors. Later, once the pool is big enough, build a lookalike audience from it.

    Capture Needed

    Meta Ads Manager → Audiences → Create audience → Custom audience → Website source dialog (owner session).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Write Two Ads That Differ Only in Angle

    Generate both from your conversion engine so they share the offer:

    • Ad A, benefit-led: the outcome your buyer wants.
    • Ad B, problem-led: their objection, in their own words.

    Same image style, same page, same audience. Tag each link with utm_source=meta (or google), utm_medium=paid and utm_content=variant_a or variant_b.

    Capture Needed

    Two finished ad creatives side by side (variant A and variant B), anonymised.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  6. 6
    Launch on the Smallest Budget

    Create the campaign with a leads objective, one audience and the two ads, on the smallest daily budget the platform allows. This step spends money as soon as the campaign is active.

    Change one variable per test. Never change the budget and the creative in the same week.

    Capture Needed

    Meta Ads Manager campaign creation with the leads objective selected (owner session).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Test Before You Trust It

    Before the ads spend a real budget, check your pages at 375px, 768px and 1280px, do a real test registration yourself, and confirm the conversion shows up in both Meta and Google.

    Then leave it alone. Reading results after four hours is how people kill ads that were working.

    Capture Needed

    Meta Events Manager → Test events showing a live Lead event from a test registration.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  8. 8
    Judge Each Ad Weekly by Cost per Lead

    Read cost per lead first. Clicks don't buy. Then apply the weekly gate:

    • Scale: click-through at least 3% and conversion at least 1.5%. Add budget, not new variables.
    • Fix today: click-through under 1%. Pause that ad.
    • Hold and tune: in between. Change exactly one thing.
    Capture Needed

    Meta Ads Manager results columns (CTR, cost per result) for two ad variants, redacted.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  9. 9
    Move the Money to the Channel That Buys

    Once a month, rank every channel by cost per buyer, not cost per click. Cost per buyer is what you spent on a channel divided by the buyers it brought.

    Move budget from the most expensive channel towards the cheapest, keeping total spend the same. Leave a small test budget on every channel, or you'll never find out when one gets cheap again.

S2

Stage 2 of 6

Landing & Registration

S2 — The Landing and Registration Page

One page: the Tantra Pro Funnel page — branded, proof-led, form above the fold. What you A/B test is the headline (benefit-led against problem-led), never a second, thinner page.

Page anatomy — what the Tantra Pro Funnel page has, and what it must not have
One page, built from one spec. Every block is switched on because it answers an objection or earns the action. If a block does neither, it comes out.
◆ Pro tip · the form abandon number is the one nobody watches

People obsess over the conversion rate and ignore form abandonment — the visitors who started typing and stopped. That number tells you something conversion rate can't: they wanted to, and something in the form stopped them. Usually it's a field you didn't need. Every field you remove is a measurable lift.

Task 3.3Build the Tantra Pro Funnel Page and the Thank-You Page

Two pages, generated from the spec:

  1. Tantra Pro Funnel page — nine blocks, form above the fold at 1366×768.
  2. Thank-you — and this one earns its keep. It confirms, it adds to calendar, it asks them to join your community group, and it sets the expectation of what arrives next. A thank-you page that only says "thanks" is a wasted asset.

Then check every page at 375px, 768px and 1280px before you call it done. Most funnel traffic is mobile, and most funnels are built on a laptop.

OwnerYou · AI builds from the specToolClaude Code + your hostTime3–5 hDeliverable2 live pages under one URL schemeProofA real registration lands in your CRM, from a phone
◆ What changes per funnel type · the capture page
Webinar FunnelThe date block is load-bearing — timezone handling, an add-to-calendar button, and a countdown. Get the timezone wrong and your show-up rate collapses for reasons you'll never diagnose.
Workshop · ChallengeThe page is a checkout, not a form. Wallets first, card below, order summary on top — and the three-day commitment stated plainly, because setting the expectation is what protects your completion rate.
Reverse SqueezeThere is no form on the entry page at all. The page is Part 1, and the opt-in bridge only appears once they've consumed enough of it to owe you an answer.
Other types: book-a-call funnels replace the form with a calendar embed plus qualification fields · free-plus-shipping needs a full address form, so every removable field matters twice as much · a final-funnel has no page at all — the "capture" is a reply in an inbox.

S2 · Landing & Registration

The Tantra Pro Funnel

Landing page, form, thank-you page, calendar file, tracking and CRM hand-off, with every automation.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Turn a click into a registered attendee in your CRM, in one step, with nothing typed by hand. You'll set up the event, build a nine-block landing page with the form above the fold, handle the form on your server so it registers the person, creates the contact, adds a calendar hold and logs the row, then send them to a thank-you page that earns its keep. You're done when a registration made from your phone appears in your event platform and your CRM with its UTM intact, and the confirmation email with the calendar file arrives.

Steps
11
Examples
11
Runs On
GA4 · LinkedIn · Vercel · Claude Code · WebinarGeek · GoHighLevel · Google Calendar · Google Sheets

How This Changes by Mechanism

The form is the conversion. The date block does the heavy lifting: the time in the visitor's time zone, an add-to-calendar button and a countdown. Get the time zone wrong and show-up drops for reasons you'll never find. The page hands straight to the event platform's registration: one list, one join link.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Set Up the Event First

    In your event platform (WebinarGeek in this stack), open Webinars → Create webinar:

    1. Choose live, write the title (a promise with a number in it) and the description.
    2. Create the episode, then the broadcast: date, time and time zone.
    3. Set the duration correctly. Every calendar entry and reminder is built from it, so a wrong duration makes every invite end at the wrong time.
    4. Decide the replay now, not after the event.
    5. Note the broadcast ID from the page address. Everything downstream keys on it.

    Tip A broadcast's date can only be changed in the web screen, not through the API. After any change, re-open it and check.

  2. 2
    Build the Landing Page From One Spec

    Write one spec and have Claude Code build the page from it. The page has nine blocks, in this order:

    1. Logo and a trust strip
    2. Headline (the promise) and subhead (the mechanism in one line)
    3. A 60–90 second video, muted, with captions
    4. Three proof points: numbers, not adjectives
    5. The registration form
    6. Your mechanism, named, in 3–5 steps
    7. Testimonials, each answering one objection
    8. An FAQ that is your objection list, answered
    9. A call-to-action button that follows the reader down the page
  3. 3
    Put the Form Where Nobody Has to Look for It

    The form sits above the fold on a 1366×768 laptop, without scrolling, and again further down the page.

    Ask only what you'll use: first name, last name, business email, and a profile link for follow-up. Ask for a phone number only if you will actually call or text.

    Watch form abandonment: people who start typing and stop. It usually points to one field you didn't need.

  4. 4
    Handle the Form on Your Server

    Never send the form straight from the browser to your tools. Send it to your own small backend, which Claude Code builds for you. In order, it:

    1. Checks every field again on the server.
    2. Registers the person in your event platform.
    3. Creates or updates the contact in your CRM.
    4. Adds a calendar hold for the session.
    5. Logs the row in a sheet.
    6. Sends the browser to the thank-you page.

    Keep every key on the server. Nothing secret belongs in the page.

  5. 5
    Make the Thank-You Page Earn Its Keep

    A thank-you page that only says 'thanks' is a wasted asset. Give it four jobs:

    1. Confirm the registration.
    2. Add to calendar: a Google Calendar button and a downloadable calendar file for everything else.
    3. Ask them to join your community group.
    4. Say exactly what arrives next and when.
  6. 6
    Send the Confirmation With the Calendar File

    Your event platform sends the confirmation the moment someone registers. Open its Emails settings for this webinar and check:

    • The date, time and join link are right.
    • The merge fields fill in. Send yourself a preview to be sure.
    • The calendar file is attached, in the registrant's time zone.
  7. 7
    Carry the UTM All the Way to the CRM

    The tag on the link that brought someone in has to reach their CRM record.

    • Read utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign and utm_content from the page address and send them with the form.
    • Save them on the contact, along with source and mechanism.
    • Add your analytics tag to every page, and mark the registration as a key event.
  8. 8
    Hand Every Registrant to the CRM the Same Way

    Every new registrant carries the same fields and the tag registered. Name the tags once and never rename them: registered, attended, no-show, purchased, plus replay-watched. Everything in Stage 3 keys off them.

    When you import a list into the CRM, match the column names to the field names exactly and choose do not overwrite existing values. A thin registration record must never replace richer data.

  9. 9
    Catch Social Lead Forms Too

    People who register through a social event page or lead form must land in the same place. An automation watches for new lead-form entries and:

    1. Checks the email isn't already registered.
    2. If it's new, does the same writes as your page: register, contact, calendar hold, log.
    3. If they're already registered, does nothing, so nobody gets two confirmations.
    Capture Needed

    The registration log sheet showing rows from both the page and a social lead form, with a source column (anonymised).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  10. 10
    Check the Live Page Every Cycle

    Before you send any traffic, open the live page:

    • The date is this event's date.
    • A test registration reaches the event platform and the CRM.
    • View Source: no keys or private tokens anywhere in the page.
    • Paste the link into a chat app. Link previews don't run scripts, so if the date is added by script, the preview shows the old one.
    • Check it at 375px, 768px and 1280px. Most funnel traffic is mobile.
  11. 11
    Register From Your Phone and Follow It Through

    The proof the funnel works is one real registration, made from a phone:

    1. Register with a test address from a tagged link.
    2. Check the thank-you page loaded and the calendar button works.
    3. Check the person is in your event platform and your CRM, with the UTM on the record.
    4. Check the confirmation email arrived with the calendar file.

    If any of the four fails, the funnel isn't live yet.

Build the Registration Backend
Build a small server endpoint for my registration form. On each submission: validate first name, last name, business email (and phone only if present) on the server; register the person for my event (broadcast ID: [id]) in my event platform; create or update the contact in my CRM with source, utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content, mechanism and the tag 'registered', never overwriting a field that already has a value; add a calendar hold; append a row to my registration log sheet; then redirect to [thank-you URL]. If the email is already registered, skip the writes and still redirect. Keep all keys in environment variables, never in the page. Show me a test run with two submissions, one new and one duplicate.

Why Costs Explode

H2: Six structural patterns. Not one bad job.
Runaway Databricks spend almost never comes from a single culprit. It's a handful of quiet, repeatable patterns compounding month over month.
1. 1. Idle and off hours waste. Interactive clusters run 24/7 at 1 to 2% peak CPU, with no auto shutdown for nights, weekends, or non production.
2. 2. Premium compute misalignment. Photon applied by default adds a 2x DBU premium on simple ETL and I/O tasks with no measurable return.
3. 3. Failed run and retry leakage. Workspaces can burn up to 57 to 63% of spend on jobs that fail after consuming full compute, with no fail fast timeouts.
4. 4. Setup and spin up dominance. High frequency micro batch jobs can spend up to 65 to 75% of runtime spinning up clusters rather than processing data.
5. 5. Small file and storage overhead. Uncompacted Delta files create I/O choke points. Thousands of tiny files inflate compute uptime.
6. 6. Governance and guardrail gaps. No tagging, no budget alerts, no compute policies. Costs drift quietly until the bill arrives.

The Framework

H2: Three tiers, one discipline.
See the spend, control the spend, guard the spend. This is the exact sequence covered in the masterclass.
Tier 1, see it. Ops and finance observability.
Query billing and job cost system tables for granular spend by SKU, job, and serverless usage. Enforce tagging by business unit, project, and environment, to the point where untagged clusters fail to launch.
Tier 2, control it. Active optimization.
Shift interactive workloads to job clusters and reserve Photon for Gold layer aggregations. Enable Delta auto optimize and scheduled compaction to remove small file overhead.
Tier 3, guard it. Ongoing governance.
Budget alerts at 50, 75 and 90% thresholds in the Databricks account console. Compute policies mandating auto termination, instance limits, and tag enforcement.

Customer Spotlight

H2: A healthcare firm cut Databricks TCO by roughly 50%.
Same workloads, same SLAs, right sized compute, no re architecture.
The situation

  • Interactive clusters ran 24/7 at roughly 2% peak CPU with no scheduled shutdown
  • Photon was enabled broadly across I/O bound ingestion jobs, paying a 2x DBU premium with no speed benefit
  • No auto termination, tagging, or budget alerts across non production workspaces

The fix

  • Right sized clusters with global auto termination on all interactive compute
  • Moved scheduled batch and ETL to job clusters, disabled Photon outside Gold layer aggregations
  • Org wide tagging, budget alerts, and compute policies for continuous governance

Result: roughly 50% reduction in Databricks TCO.

S3

Stage 3 of 6

Multi-Channel Nurture

S3 — The Nurture Engine (Where Show-Up Is Won)

Here's the number nobody wants to hear: roughly half the people who register never turn up. Not because your content is bad — they haven't seen it yet. Because life happened and nothing reminded them hard enough.

Nurture is the cheapest lift in the entire funnel. You already paid to acquire these people. Every reminder that converts a registration into an attendee costs you almost nothing and is worth exactly as much as a new lead.

The Tantra Pro Flow — six touches before, two branches after
The no-show branch is worth more than it looks. These people registered — they raised their hand and then life got in the way. They are not cold, and treating them like a lost cause is the most common unforced error in the whole funnel.
◆ Do this · send the T−24h reminder at 8am in their timezone

Not 8am in yours. A reminder that lands at 3am is a reminder that gets buried under everything that arrived after it. If your tool can't send by recipient timezone, that's a reason to change tools — this single setting moves show-up more than most copy changes will.

Task 3.4Write the Tantra Pro Flow and Set the Send Windows

Generate all of it from the engine, then set the mechanics by hand:

  • Word counts matter. The T−24h email can be 180–220 words. The T−1h is 80–100. The "we're live" is 50–70 and contains one link. People skim in inverse proportion to urgency.
  • Every message has exactly one link. Two links is a decision, and a decision at T−15 minutes is a lost attendee.
  • Run every draft through a spam checker before it goes near a real list.
  • Set the branch tags — registered, attended, no-show, replay-watched. Everything downstream keys off these, so name them once and never rename them.
OwnerYou · AI drafts, you set timingsToolEmail + messaging platformTime3 hDeliverable14-node Tantra Pro Flow, liveProofYou register as a test contact and receive every touch, on time
◆ What changes per funnel type · nurture
Webinar FunnelPurely time-triggered off one date. Build it once and every future run reuses it — change the date in the spec and all six touches move together.
Workshop · ChallengeThree nested copies of the same shape, plus the daily delivery loop: recap → the artifact they generated → what tomorrow needs. Non-completion on day two is your early-warning signal for churn.
Reverse SqueezeNot time-triggered at all — depth-triggered. Under 25% of Part 1 gets a re-engage; 25–75% gets the missing-piece nudge; over 75% goes straight to the Part 2 bridge.
Other types: book-a-call funnels replace show-up nurture with no-show rebooking, which recovers a meaningful slice of bookings · product launches run a dated open-cart countdown · free-plus-shipping switches nurture to post-purchase entirely, because the sale already happened.

S3 · Multi-Channel Nurture

The Tantra Pro Flow

Six timed touches before the session, then an attended or no-show branch, across four channels.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Get registrants to actually turn up, then follow up with each person based on what they did. You'll send six timed touches across email, WhatsApp, SMS and an AI voice call, then split everyone into an attended branch and a no-show branch, and finally hand them all to the 52-week cadence. A scheduler and a set of behaviour tags run it without anyone pressing send. You're done when a test contact who attends and a test contact who deliberately misses both receive every touch on time and get the right tag automatically.

Steps
14
Examples
12
Runs On
WebinarGeek · Claude Code · GoHighLevel · Gmail · WhatsApp · Twilio · ElevenLabs

How This Changes by Mechanism

Purely time-triggered off one date: confirmation, T−7 days, T−24 hours at 8am their time, T−1 hour, T−15 minutes, then T−0 with SMS and the AI voice call added. Change the date in the spec and every touch moves together. Afterwards, attended people get the +0 offer and booking link, and no-shows get the replay after 24 hours with a real expiry.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Name Your Tags Once

    Everything in this flow keys off tags on the contact. Name them once and never rename them:

    • registered: set by your page in Stage 2.
    • attended and no-show: set from your event platform after the session.
    • replay-watched: set when someone watches the replay.
    • purchased: set in Stage 5.

    A typo in a tag silently breaks every automation that listens for it.

  2. 2
    Collect Channel Opt-Ins on the Form

    Only message people on channels they agreed to. Add a tick box for WhatsApp and one for texts and calls on the registration form, and save them as tags on the contact (for example whatsapp_reminder).

    The scheduler only messages contacts with the matching opt-in tag.

  3. 3
    Turn on the Event Platform's Own Emails

    Your event platform sends the confirmation and reminders natively. In WebinarGeek, open the webinar's Emails and check the confirmation, the 1-day, the 1-hour and the live email. Send yourself a preview of each.

    If you move the broadcast, these send times don't move with it. Cancel the planned emails and reschedule them.

  4. 4
    Write Every Touch With One Link

    Generate every message from your conversion engine, then set the mechanics by hand:

    • T−24 hours: 180–220 words. What to prepare before joining.
    • T−1 hour: 80–100 words. The join link, again.
    • We're live: 50–70 words, one link.

    Every message has exactly one link. Two links is a decision, and a decision at T−15 minutes is a lost attendee. Run every draft through a spam checker before it goes near a real list.

  5. 5
    Send the T−24 Hour Reminder at 8am Their Time

    Not 8am in yours. A reminder that lands at 3am gets buried under everything that arrives after it.

    Store each registrant's time zone and send by it. If your tool can't send by the recipient's time zone, that's a reason to change tools. This one setting moves show-up more than most copy changes.

    Capture Needed

    A CRM workflow or scheduler setting that sends in the contact's own time zone.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  6. 6
    Set Up WhatsApp and SMS Messages

    Business WhatsApp messages sent first have to use an approved template. In Twilio, open the Content Template Builder, create a template for each reminder (T−24h, T−1h, T−15m, live) with the join link as a variable, and submit it for approval.

    Keep SMS to the last hour: T−1h and T−15m, one link each, and only to people who opted in to texts. Check Twilio's sending requirements for your registrants' countries before the first send.

  7. 7
    Build the Reminder Scheduler

    Clocks don't send webhooks, so a scheduler checks every 5 minutes:

    1. Find the next session and the minutes left until it starts.
    2. If it's within ±3 minutes of a reminder window (24h, 1h, 15m, live, then +1, +2 and +3 days), pick the contacts for that session who opted in.
    3. Skip anyone whose session ID doesn't match, so nobody gets another event's reminder.
    4. Tag them for that reminder; the tag triggers the send.
    5. Wait between batches, or messaging apps flag you.

    Claude Code builds this from the prompt below. No n8n or Zapier needed.

    Capture Needed

    The reminder scheduler's run log showing a window match and the number of contacts tagged (anonymised).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  8. 8
    Add the AI Voice Call at Go-Live

    At T−0, an AI voice call reaches the people who still haven't joined. Keep it under 30 seconds: who's calling, that the session is starting now, and that the link is in their WhatsApp and email.

    Call only people who opted in, say plainly that it's an automated call, and stop calling anyone who says no. ElevenLabs supplies the voice.

  9. 9
    Turn What They Did Into Tags

    After the session, your event platform reports who joined live, who watched the replay and who didn't show. An automation listens for each event, finds the contact in your CRM and applies the matching tag.

    Don't trust tags alone for who attended. Check viewing time too: 'did not watch' in the data doesn't always mean 'did not attend'. Filtering on the wrong flag has sent 'sorry you missed it' to people who watched the whole thing.

  10. 10
    Build the Attended Branch

    They've seen the offer. Four touches:

    1. +0: the offer and the booking link, sent while they're still in the room.
    2. +1 day: a recap and the first objection from your buyer profile, answered.
    3. +2 days: proof and the second objection: a named result, not an adjective.
    4. +3 days: last call, with a real deadline. If there's no deadline, don't use the words.
  11. 11
    Build the No-Show Branch

    They registered, so they're not cold. Four touches:

    1. +24 hours: the replay, with an expiry. No expiry means no reason to watch today.
    2. +2 days: the one thing they missed: one idea, with its timestamp, not 'here's the recording'.
    3. +5 days: the replay closes tonight. Then actually close it.
    4. Still nothing: the 30-day nurture. Unqualified is not the same as uninterested.
  12. 12
    Attach Each Email Template by Hand

    In GoHighLevel, build each email under Marketing → Emails → Templates, inside a folder. Templates in a folder don't show at the top level, so open the folder to find them.

    Then open Marketing → Automation → Workflows, open the workflow, click the email action and pick the template. This step can't be done through the API. It's always manual.

  13. 13
    Test It as Two Registrants
    1. Register as a test contact and attend. Check you get every touch, on time, and the attended tag lands.
    2. Register again with a second address and deliberately don't show. Check the no-show tag lands and the replay email arrives.

    Nobody should touch anything for either test to pass.

    Capture Needed

    Two test contacts in the CRM, one tagged attended and one tagged no-show, with their message history (redacted).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  14. 14
    Move Everyone Into the 52-Week Cadence

    Nobody leaves the funnel. They just change speed. When the attended branch ends, or the no-show branch reaches the 30-day nurture, everyone still on your list moves into the 52-week cadence in Stage 6.

    Capture Needed

    The CRM workflow's final step moving contacts into the long-term newsletter list.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

Build the Reminder Scheduler
Build a scheduled job that runs every 5 minutes. Each run: fetch my next upcoming session from my event platform (broadcast ID and start time); compute minutes until start; if it is within ±3 minutes of one of these windows: 1440, 60, 15, 0 minutes before, or 1, 2, 3 days after, find CRM contacts whose broadcast_id matches and who carry the opt-in tag for the channel; add the window's tag (1_day_reminder, 1_hour_reminder, 15_min_reminder, going_live_reminder, followup_day_1/2/3) so my CRM workflow sends the message; format the date and time in each contact's own time zone; never tag the same contact twice for the same window; pause between batches. Log every run. Show me a dry run against a session starting in 61 minutes.

Conversion Mechanism

S4 — The Live Delivery

Everything so far was preparation for sixty minutes. Run those sixty minutes off a script and a clock, not off vibes — because the moments that produce bookings happen at specific times, and if you're improvising you'll miss them.

Run of show — sixty minutes, four lanes, nothing improvised
Do a full dry run. Same platform, same slides, same polls, a test attendee on a second device. Every failure you find in rehearsal costs you nothing; the same failure live costs you the room.
Task 3.5Write the Run of Show, the Script and the Four Polls

Three artifacts, all generated from the engine and then hand-tuned:

  1. Run of show — the timeline above, with your actual slide numbers written against each marker.
  2. The script — not word-for-word, but every transition written out. The three places people fumble are the open, the move from teaching into the offer, and the close of Q&A. Write those three verbatim.
  3. Four polls, in this order: persona, challenge, investment priority, discovery-call interest — these are your diagnostic from Day 1, in live form. Poll answers are the strongest intent signal of the whole session, so make sure they land in the CRM tagged, not in a screenshot.

Then assign the five roles to actual names. A role with nobody's name on it is a role nobody does.

S4 · Conversion MechanismWebinar

The Live Webinar

Set up the room, rehearse it, run sixty minutes on a clock, and close while people are still watching.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Set up one live webinar room, staff it with named roles, rehearse it, then run sixty minutes on a fixed clock: 45 minutes of teaching, 15 of Q&A, and the offer landing once near the end. Every registration, attendance and poll answer flows into your CRM as a tag. Done means a dry run has recorded, the offer button fires at its minute, and a test attendee arrives in the CRM tagged attended.

Steps
14
Examples
11
Runs On
WebinarGeek · DenchClaw CRM · Cal.com · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Create the Webinar Room

    In your webinar tool, create a new live webinar (everyone joins at the same time). Give it the same title, date and time as your registration page, and set the length to 60 minutes.

    • Pick the Webinar format, so attendees watch and presenters are on stage.
    • Check the timezone shown next to the date. It's the one reminders will use.
    • Leave replays switched on; you'll set their expiry in step 12.

    Tip Zoom works too: Webinars → Schedule a Webinar, registration Required, practice session on, record to the cloud.

  2. 2
    Ask Only for the Fields You Will Use

    Registration fields decide what you can do later. Use the playbook's five, and nothing more:

    1. First name
    2. Last name
    3. Business email
    4. Profile link (so the team can follow up personally)
    5. Phone, only if you will call or text

    If people register on your own page (the Tantra Pro Funnel), send those fields to the webinar tool, so there's one list and one join link per person.

    Tip Every extra field costs registrations. Ask the rest after they've said yes.

  3. 3
    Send Every Event to Your CRM

    Add one webhook per event, pointing at your CRM or automation endpoint. Each one sets a tag that Stages 3 and 5 key off:

    • New registration → registered
    • New live viewer → attended
    • No show → no-show
    • New replay viewer → replay-watched

    The webinar tool is the only system that knows who really watched, so this step is what makes every follow-up personal.

  4. 4
    Put Five Names on Five Roles

    The host only teaches. Four more people run the room, and each role gets a real name before the day:

    1. Host: teaches and makes the offer.
    2. Content moderator: watches the clock and relays questions.
    3. Tech moderator: stage, screens, anyone who can't hear.
    4. Chat and Q&A: posts the link, clears spam, marks answered questions.
    5. DM operator: sends the 1:1 messages at minutes 3, 15 and 40.

    Add them as co-presenters or moderators, and keep a team-only chat open backstage.

    Tip A role without a name on it doesn't get done. One person can cover two roles; nobody covers three.

  5. 5
    Build the Four Polls Before the Day

    Four polls, in this order, each doing one job:

    1. Persona: on slide 1. Who's in the room.
    2. Challenge: early. The main problem, in their words.
    3. Investment priority: around minute 10 to 15. Separates browsers from buyers.
    4. Discovery-call interest: on the pitch slide. This is the list your close follows up.

    Create all four as interactions now, so launching one live is a single click.

  6. 6
    Add the Offer Button and Set Its Minute

    Create a Call to action interaction. Choose Open a URL and paste your booking link (offer about $1,000 or more) or your checkout link (under that). Add ?src=live to the link, so the sale is credited to the session.

    Set its start time to the minute your offer slide appears, and let it stay up to the end of the hour.

    Tip The offer lands once. Don't show the button during the teaching.

  7. 7
    Open Q&A With Upvotes

    Set Q&A to Public, so attendees can see and upvote each other's questions. Answer the most-voted first. If the room is quiet, the host answers three to five common questions openly, as questions people often ask. Never post questions under invented attendee names.

  8. 8
    Turn Recording On

    Turn on recording for live webinars before the day. The recording becomes your replay, your no-show recovery and your next month's clips. Say "this is recorded" out loud during the session.

  9. 9
    Run a Full Dry Run Two to Three Days Before

    Same computer, same network, same room, same slides. Walk the whole hour:

    • Every presenter reaches the stage, with the right name showing.
    • A test attendee joins on a second device, to see what they see.
    • Each poll fires, the offer button appears at its minute, the recording lands.
    • Hand-offs between roles are agreed out loud.

    On the morning, make a second person co-host as a fallback.

    Tip Every failure you find in the dry run costs nothing. The same failure live costs the room.

  10. 10
    Run the Hour on the Clock

    Go live on the hour. The clock runs the session, not the mood in the room:

    1. 0–5: doors open; ask where people are joining from.
    2. 5–10: who this is for, why to stay to the end, poll 1.
    3. 10–45: teaching; poll 2 early, poll 3 around minute 10 to 15.
    4. Near 45: the offer, once; poll 4 on the pitch slide.
    5. 45–60: Q&A by upvotes, then close by repeating the offer.

    Meanwhile, chat posts the link every 5 minutes after the offer, and the DM operator messages at minutes 3, 15 and 40.

  11. 11
    Close While They Are Still in the Room

    At the offer minute the button appears on stage for everyone. Then:

    • Anyone who answered yes to poll 4 gets a personal message with the booking link within the hour.
    • The link stays pinned in chat until the end.
    • The deadline you name is real, and it's the same one on the slide and in every email.
  12. 12
    Give the Replay a Real Expiry

    Turn on Availability and set the date the replay closes. Then close it on that date. People who missed it get the replay 24 hours later, and the Tantra Pro Flow tells them when it closes.

  13. 13
    Export the Reports and Tag Everyone

    Straight after the hour, export three reports: registrants, attendees (with minutes watched), and poll answers per person. Check the CRM has the same people tagged attended and no-show, and add each person's poll 4 answer.

    These tags start the attended branch and the no-show branch of the Tantra Pro Flow, and the Stage 5 close chain.

  14. 14
    Copy the Webinar for the Next Run

    Copy this webinar, emails, interactions and presentation included, and only change the date. Each new run then takes minutes, not a rebuild. Move the old event page's date to the new one before the current session starts, so its listing keeps its attendees.

Write My Run of Show
Write a 60-minute run of show for a live webinar: 45 minutes of teaching and 15 of Q&A, with the offer landing once near minute 45. Put four polls in this order: persona (slide 1), challenge (early), investment priority (minute 10–15), discovery-call interest (pitch slide). Add chat prompts, the DM operator's messages at minutes 3, 15 and 40, and who does what in each minute.

My offer: {offer_name}. My buyer: {icp_role}. Their main problem: {pain_point}. My method: {mechanism_name}.
Write My Four Polls
Write the four live-webinar polls for {event_title}: persona, challenge, investment priority and discovery-call interest. Three or four answers each, in plain words a {icp_role} would use. Poll 4 must separate "book me now" from "not yet".

Webinar Framework: How to Use Salesforce AI to Cut Down Customer Service Costs by 70% in 2026

Approach 1: Process Optimization (Augmentation Model)

What It Means:
This approach enhances existing workflows without fundamentally changing how support operates. AI acts as an intelligent assistant that accelerates human work—making agents faster, more consistent, and more effective.
How It Works:

  • AI assists human agents in real-time during customer interactions
  • Systems retrieve relevant information, suggest responses, and summarize context
  • Humans remain in control of all decisions and final outputs
  • Current processes stay largely intact; speed and accuracy improve

Typical Use Cases:

  • Intelligent response drafting: AI suggests contextual replies based on ticket history and knowledge base
  • Automated case summarization: Converting long conversation threads into digestible summaries
  • Smart information retrieval: Surfacing relevant help articles, previous tickets, or account details instantly
  • Assisted troubleshooting: Guiding agents through diagnostic steps with contextual prompts
  • Example: Intelligent shipment tracking with human review before customer response

Cost Reduction Mechanism:
Reduce Average Handle Time (AHT) by accelerating information access and reducing manual writing. Lower training time for new agents through embedded guidance systems.
Risk Profile: Low
Human oversight remains constant. Errors are caught before reaching customers. Rollback is straightforward if issues arise.
Best Starting Point For:

  • Organizations new to AI in customer service
  • Highly regulated industries requiring human oversight
  • Teams with complex, judgment-heavy support scenarios
  • Companies without mature data infrastructure
Approach 2: Process Reimagination (Automation Model)

What It Means:
This approach redesigns workflows from the ground up, eliminating entire categories of human work. AI doesn't just assist—it independently handles complete processes end-to-end.
How It Works:

  • AI systems operate autonomously within defined boundaries
  • Certain ticket types or request categories are fully automated
  • Humans are removed from routine workflows entirely
  • Escalation to humans occurs only when confidence thresholds aren't met

Typical Use Cases:

  • Autonomous policy verification: Checking eligibility, coverage, or compliance without human review
  • Self-service order modifications: Processing returns, cancellations, or changes automatically
  • Automated account provisioning: Creating accounts, setting permissions, sending credentials
  • Multi-step approval workflows: Routing requests through validation chains without manual touchpoints
  • Example: Automated Smart Analysis, where complex policy checks, approvals, or multi-step analyses happen in the background

Cost Reduction Mechanism:
Eliminate high percentages of routine ticket volume by fully automating high-frequency, low-complexity requests. Redirect human agents exclusively to complex, high-value interactions.
Risk Profile: Medium to High
Requires robust data quality, clear decision logic, and strong governance. Mistakes directly impact customers. Requires sophisticated monitoring and fallback systems.
Best Starting Point For:

  • Organizations with mature data infrastructure
  • High-volume, repetitive support workflows
  • Companies with clear, rule-based processes
  • Teams ready for organizational change management
Part 1: The Progressive Adoption Framework

Why Traditional Support Models Fail to Scale Cost-Effectively
Most support organizations operate on a fundamentally linear model:

  • More volume = More agents = More cost
  • Agent productivity plateaus after initial training
  • Knowledge fragmentation leads to inconsistent quality
  • Manual processes create bottlenecks that can't be optimized away

The result: support costs scale in direct proportion to growth, consuming increasing percentages of revenue over time.
The AI-Driven Alternative: The Agent Maturity Ladder
Rather than choosing between full automation and no automation, successful organizations follow a progressive maturity path:
AI Providing Information → AI Making Decisions → AI Taking Autonomous Actions
Level 1: AI Providing Information
AI retrieves and surfaces relevant information to human agents. Agents make all decisions and take all actions.
Role: Information assistant
Level 2: AI Making Decisions
AI analyzes situations, evaluates options, and recommends specific actions. Humans review recommendations and choose whether to act.
Role: Decision advisor
Level 3: AI Taking Autonomous Actions
AI independently executes complete workflows within defined boundaries. Humans monitor exceptions and handle escalations only.
Role: Autonomous operator
Strategic Insight: Build Trust Before Scaling
Organizations that achieve significant cost reduction don't jump directly to autonomous actions. They:
1. Begin with information assistance to build confidence and gather operational data
2. Progress to decision support as trust and accuracy improve
3. Expand to autonomous actions only for specific, well-understood use cases
4. Scale systematically based on performance data and user feedback
5. Continuously optimize across all maturity levels
Key Principle:
Transitioning from "outputs" to "actions" requires building trust at each level before progressing.

Part 3: The 4-Step Implementation Methodology

This framework outlines how to build an autonomous support operation within the Salesforce ecosystem.

Step 1: Identifying High-ROI Use Cases

Objective: Find the right starting point—avoid "big bang" rollouts that create excessive risk.
The Use Case Selection Framework:
Use an Impact vs. Feasibility Matrix to evaluate opportunities systematically.
Impact Assessment: Prioritize tasks that align with:

  • Cost reduction: Which use cases eliminate the most manual work?
  • Volume management: Which handles the highest ticket volumes?

Feasibility Assessment: Evaluate based on:

  • Data quality: Is the necessary data accurate, complete, and accessible?
  • Existing API connectivity: Can AI access required systems without major integration work?

Target Zone: Focus on opportunities in the "quick-win" quadrant—high impact on costs and volume, combined with strong data quality and API readiness.

Data-Backed Prioritization

When multiple use cases appear equally promising or stakeholder preferences conflict:
Incorporate quantitative evidence:

  • Current process volume
  • Average handling time
  • Error rates
  • Customer satisfaction scores
  • Resolution rates
  • Revenue leakage metrics

Purpose:
Historical performance data helps objectively rank opportunities, resolve disagreements, and select the highest-ROI starting point.

Strategic Implementation Approach

Start Small, Prove Value, Then Expand:
1. Begin with assistive and semi-autonomous use cases
2. Focus on opportunities that are high-impact, low-to-medium effort, and low-risk
3. Target use cases where AI augments human work without requiring full autonomy from day one
4. Deliver measurable ROI rapidly (often in weeks to months)
5. Build internal confidence and minimize risks around adoption, compliance, or integration
6. Use early success as foundation for expanding to more complex workflows
This approach:

  • Avoids common pitfalls like over-ambitious projects or unclear value
  • Enables a scalable path from pilots to enterprise-wide transformation
  • Reduces risks around adoption, compliance, and integration
Step 2: Designing the Reasoning Logic

Core Principle:
Leaders must decide how the agent "thinks" before it acts.
Fundamental Question:
Not every agent needs reasoning—but every agent needs clarity about its decision-making approach.
Determine:

  • Is this a reactive agent (retrieve, summarize, respond)?
  • Or a decision-making agent that plans, evaluates, or chooses?

This leads to two key design choices:

Choice 1: Deterministic Logic vs. Probabilistic Judgment

Deterministic Logic
Probabilistic Judgment
Fixed rules for specific outcomes
Model-driven inference
Same input → same outcome
Likelihood-based outcomes
Best for: Compliance checks, specific approvals, validations, routing
Best for: Interpreting customer intent, providing recommendations, understanding context
Implementation Guidance:
Use Deterministic Logic when:

  • Regulatory requirements mandate specific workflows
  • Financial transactions require zero-tolerance accuracy
  • Compliance checks must be fully auditable
  • Approval processes follow explicit organizational rules

Use Probabilistic Judgment when:

  • Understanding customer requests from free-text input
  • Personalizing responses based on context and history
  • Recommending next-best actions
  • Interpreting ambiguous situations

Common Production Pattern:
Most production agents blend both approaches:

  • Deterministic rules decide when to act
  • Probabilistic models decide how to respond
Choice 2: Explicit Decision Trees vs. Implicit Chain-of-Thought

Explicit Decision Trees
Implicit Chain-of-Thought
You define every reasoning path
The model reasons internally
Transparent, auditable, predictable
Flexible and adaptive, but harder to explain and control
When to Use Which:

  • Use explicit trees when you need full auditability (healthcare, finance, insurance)
  • Use implicit reasoning when flexibility matters more than perfect transparency
Prompting Strategy

Model choice is a design decision—not a default.
Consider:

  • Reasoning-heavy vs. language-heavy tasks
  • Latency-sensitive vs. depth-sensitive use cases
  • Cost vs. accuracy trade-offs

Prompting Techniques and When to Use Them:
Technique
Use Case
Zero-shot prompting
Simple, well-defined tasks (summaries, classifications)
Few-shot prompting
When consistency, tone, or structure matters
Instruction + constraints prompting
When outputs must follow strict rules or formats
Tool / function calling
When the agent must act or fetch live data
Step-based or decomposed prompting
For multi-step decisions, prioritization, or planning
Key Principle:
Good prompts reduce ambiguity, cost, and surprises.

Step 3: Automated Validation and Testing

Core Reality:
Manual testing is no longer sufficient for dynamic AI.

Why Traditional Testing Fails for AI

As AI agents move beyond static workflows and operate across dynamic, conversational paths, testing becomes exponentially more complex.
The Complexity Problem:
Agentic AI workflows:

  • Can execute the same task in multiple valid ways
  • Trigger different paths based on context, data, or user input
  • Interact dynamically with APIs, systems, and policies

At scale, this results in:

  • A vast number of workflow permutations
  • Variations driven by user demographics, languages, and behaviors
  • Edge cases that surface only in real-world usage

The Limitation:
Traditional testing approaches struggle to keep up. It becomes nearly impossible to predefine and validate every scenario using static test cases or manual scripts. Manual testing becomes impractical for Agentic AI at scale.

The Solution: AI-Testing-AI Methodology

Approach:
Use AI-driven testing—AI systems designed specifically to test and validate other AI agents.
How It Works:
1. Synthetic Data Generation:

  • AI generates realistic customer interactions automatically
  • Creates hundreds or thousands of test scenarios in real time
  • Covers positive scenarios, negative cases, and edge conditions

2. Automated Workflow Testing:

  • Stress-test agents across all scenario types
  • Test different conversation paths and decision branches
  • Validate behavior under various conditions

3. Validation Against Human Baselines:

  • Compare AI agent responses to historical human agent outcomes
  • Ensure AI performs at human-comparable levels
  • Identify gaps where AI underperforms

4. Scale Measurement:

  • Measure accuracy, reliability, and consistency at scale
  • Track success rates across thousands of test interactions
  • Validate integration robustness
Testing Scope

Using standard testing platforms and frameworks:

  • Validate agent behavior across predefined scenarios and edge cases
  • Test consistency and failure handling
  • Ensure the agent's "Actions" stage matches organizational standards
  • Verify integration robustness across systems
  • Confirm agents meet baseline functional and performance expectations

Outcome:
This combined approach ensures agents don't just work technically, but perform at a human-comparable level in real operational conditions.

Step 4: Phased Deployment and Adoption

Core Principle:
Adoption is not automatic. Transitioning from "outputs" to "actions" requires building trust.

Rollout Strategy

Requirement:
AI requires phased activation, not big-bang releases.
Implementation Approach:

  • Controlled rollout by use case or user group
  • Clear fallback and escalation paths
  • Defined ownership for agent behavior

Progressive Rollout Pattern:
1. Start with internal testing (small group of support agents)
2. Pilot with low-risk customer segments
3. Monitor closely and iterate
4. Expand gradually based on performance data
5. Maintain fallback paths throughout

Training: Teaching Trust and Override

Focus Areas:

  • Video-based, role-specific training: Practical demonstrations of AI in real scenarios
  • When to trust the AI: What types of requests is AI highly reliable on?
  • When to override: When should agents intervene or correct AI outputs?
  • When to escalate: What scenarios require human judgment or supervisor involvement?
  • Setting the right expectations: AI as a co-worker, not a replacement

Key Principle:
Users must understand both capabilities and limitations to use AI effectively.

The Maturity Ladder in Practice

Level 1: AI Providing Information

  • Deploy AI to assist agents with information retrieval
  • Agents review all AI-provided information before acting
  • Build confidence in data accuracy and relevance

Level 2: AI Making Decisions

  • AI begins recommending specific actions
  • Agents review recommendations and choose whether to proceed
  • Trust increases as recommendation quality proves consistent

Level 3: AI Taking Autonomous Actions

  • AI handles specific use cases end-to-end
  • Agents monitor exceptions and handle escalations only
  • Full autonomy achieved for defined workflows

Movement Between Levels:
Progress only when performance data and user confidence support the transition.

Part 4: Operational Guardrails

To maintain safety while cutting costs, the following must be integrated into the architecture:

Guardrail 1: Security & Compliance

Requirements:

  • PII Masking: Personally Identifiable Information must be masked or redacted
  • Role-based access: What the agent can see, say, and do must be controlled by user role
  • User data protection: Customer interactions are not stored or used for model training
  • Auditability: All actions and decisions must be traceable

Especially Critical In:

  • Financial services
  • Healthcare & life sciences
  • Insurance
  • Telecom
  • Public sector and regulated enterprises

Key Principle:
Security and trust are features, not constraints.

Guardrail 2: Confidence Thresholds

Core Requirement:
The system must know when it is "unsure" and trigger a context-rich handoff to a human.
Implementation:

  • Define confidence threshold levels (e.g., <80% confidence = escalate)
  • When AI uncertainty is detected, escalate gracefully
  • Provide complete context to the human taking over:
  • Full conversation history
  • Attempted actions
  • Why AI couldn't resolve
  • Relevant customer data

Key Principle:
Clear signaling that escalation is intentional, not an error.

Guardrail 3: Fallbacks & Human Handoffs

Plan Upfront:

  • Clean, context-rich handoffs to humans
  • Confidence thresholds for escalation
  • Clear signaling to both agents and customers

Design Principle:
Well-designed agents know when to step aside.

Guardrail 4: Performance & Scale Requirements

Design For:

  • Response-time expectations
  • Concurrent usage and peak loads
  • Cost predictability
  • Dependency failures across models, APIs, or data sources

Key Takeaway:
Production agents must be resilient, not just intelligent.

Guardrail 5: Prompt and Model Governance

Requirements:

  • Versioning of all instructions and prompts
  • Approval processes for changes
  • Rollback capability when issues arise
  • Clear ownership of agent behavior

Why This Matters:
Prevents unauthorized changes and enables rapid recovery from problems.

Part 5: Measuring Outcomes & ROI

Success is measured through both operational and technical lenses.

Performance Measurement Framework

Track success using two layers of KPIs:
Operational KPIs
Metric
What It Measures
Average Handle Time (AHT)
How much faster are interactions?
First Contact Resolution (FCR)
What percentage of issues are resolved without escalation?
Customer Satisfaction (CSAT)
Are customers satisfied with AI-assisted support?

Technical KPIs

Category
Key Metrics
Adoption
Sessions, Active Users, Usage Trends
Effectiveness
Success & Escalation Rates, Quality Scores, Topic Accuracy
Reliability
Error Rate, Latency, System Uptime
Cost/ROI
Cost per Interaction, Consumption Metrics

Continuous Improvement Process

Core Principle:
AI success is not a one-time launch—it's an operating model.
What to Monitor:

  • Workflow changes
  • Data drift
  • Agent adoption patterns
  • Performance across use cases

Continuous Improvement in Action:
AI agents typically do not launch at peak performance. Initial accuracy often starts around 70%.
Improvement Process:
As real usage data becomes available:
1. Instruction tuning: Refine prompts and decision logic
2. Data quality enhancements: Fix data accuracy and completeness issues
3. Workflow refinements: Optimize processes based on observed behavior
Result:
Steady and measurable increase in accuracy over time.
Key Insight:
Organizations must treat AI as a continuously improving system, monitoring performance and iterating based on real-world data.

Part 6: Common Implementation Patterns Across Industries

Recurring Problem Patterns
Observation:
Industries change. Service problems don't.
When stripped of domain language and organizational structure, the same service patterns repeat across sectors—healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, education, consumer services, financial services, and more.
Common Patterns:
Pattern 1: Status Inquiries

  • Enquiries that boil down to checking status
  • High volume, low complexity
  • Clear data sources available
  • Ideal for autonomous handling

Pattern 2: Search vs. Resolution

  • Agents spending time searching for information instead of resolving issues
  • Knowledge fragmentation across systems
  • Opportunity for AI-assisted information retrieval

Pattern 3: Field Context Needs

  • Field teams needing fast context and frictionless logging
  • Mobile access requirements
  • Real-time data synchronization needs

Pattern 4: Volume Without Signal

  • Managers overwhelmed by volume but starved of actionable signal
  • Need for intelligent summarization and prioritization
  • Analytics to surface patterns and trends

Strategic Implication:
Solutions can be designed as reusable templates that apply across different industries with appropriate customization.

The Reverse Squeeze Funnel, End to End

Everything above assumed a dated event. A reverse squeeze has no date, no registration and no live moment — and it still runs all six stages. Here's the whole thing, at the same depth, because "it's just a landing page with a video" is how people build one that doesn't work.

The core idea: you give the valuable thing away before you ask for anything. Not a teaser. Not a preview. The actual thing. The opt-in comes afterwards, and it converts far better because by then you've earned it.

Reverse squeeze — all six stages, no date, no form up front
Notice what's missing: a date. Nothing here expires, which is why a reverse squeeze costs fewer hours to run each week — and why it takes longer to produce a result. You're trading urgency for compounding.
StageWhat you buildThe number that proves it
S1 Traffic2 variants per channel, all pointing at Part 1. No registration language anywhere — the click promise is the content itselfClicks to Part 1, per channel
S2 Part 1The content page, the asset itself, depth events at 25/50/75/100%, and the opt-in bridge with its threshold in the spec% reaching 75% depth
S3 NurtureThree depth-triggered sequences, not one time-triggered one. Each with its own hookBridge opt-in rate per depth band
S4 Part 2Gated page, instant delivery, email backup, and the escalation into the offerPart 2 completion rate
S5 OfferTwo offer pages — low-ticket and premium — plus the routing rule that decides which one they seePurchase rate, split by branch
S6 GrowthThree tracks: ascension for low-ticket buyers, a fresh Part 1 monthly for non-buyers, referral for premium buyersRepeat purchase and referral rate
◆ Pro tip · the threshold is your highest-leverage variable

Where you place the opt-in bridge decides everything downstream. Too early and you're a squeeze page wearing a costume — you lose the trust the format exists to build. Too late and people finish, feel satisfied, and leave. Put it in the spec, start around three-quarters through, and treat it as your first A/B test.

Task 3.7If You're Building a Reverse Squeeze, Build It in This Order
  1. Make Part 1 first, and make it genuinely good enough that you'd have charged for it. This is not negotiable — the entire mechanism rests on the value being real.
  2. Instrument depth before you build anything else. Without depth events you have no funnel, just a page.
  3. Build the bridge and set its threshold in the spec, not in code.
  4. Build Part 2 and the offer inside it.
  5. Then the three nurture branches, then the two offer pages and the routing rule.
  6. Traffic last. Same as every other shape.
OwnerYouToolClaude Code · video host · emailTime33 h build · 4–8 h/week to runDeliverablePart 1 · bridge · Part 2 · 3 branches · 2 offer pagesProofDepth events fire at all four milestones for a real session

S4 · Conversion MechanismReverse Squeeze Page (VSL)

The Reverse Squeeze Page

A separate page that plays your video sales letter first and asks for nothing until the viewer is deep in.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Record one video sales letter from the template, put it alone on its own page, and let it teach before it asks. A button appears at the script's off-ramp line; a short bridge form appears only once the viewer is deep in, and sends Part 2 in seconds. Every play, milestone and form is an event, so follow-up is set by how much each person watched. Done means a test viewer who reaches 75% sees the bridge, gets Part 2, and lands in the CRM with their depth on the contact.

Steps
11
Examples
8
Runs On
Claude Code · Wistia · GA4 · Vercel · Cal.com · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Generate the Script From the Template

    Open the VSL Script Template below. It has 32 beats in three acts: hook and proof, teaching that shifts five beliefs, then the offer. Every specific is a field, like {desired_outcome} or {mechanism_name}.

    • Fill the fields from your Day 1 answers: your buyer, their pain, your method, your offer.
    • Use only proof you can source. If a proof field is empty, the beat is rewritten without it.
    • Paste the filled fields into the prompt at the end of this guide to get the full script, the cue sheet and the captions.

    Tip Never invent a number, logo, rating or deadline to fill a field. Leave the beat out instead.

  2. 2
    Record Once, Cut It Three Ways

    Record the long version (35 to 50 minutes), then cut a 12-minute and a 6-minute version from it. Each beat in the template says which cuts keep it.

    For every cut, write down one number: the second the early off-ramp line starts (beat B09). That number drives the page's button. Upload two cuts as an A/B test, so the data picks the length.

  3. 3
    Host It Muted, With Captions On

    Most viewers start with the sound off. In your video host:

    • Turn autoplay on, muted, with a click for sound prompt.
    • Generate captions from the final edit, and turn them on by default.
    • Hide related videos and anything that links away.
  4. 4
    Build a Page That Is Only the Video

    This is a separate page from your registration page. It has:

    • A one-line call-out: who it's for.
    • A headline taken from beat B01 of the script.
    • The video, above the fold on a laptop and on a phone.
    • Nothing else to click: no menu, no form, no links except the legal ones in the footer.

    The workshop's own thank-you page uses the same player pattern: muted autoplay, a click-to-listen panel and captions.

    Tip Every link off the page leaks watch time. Unlink the logo too.

  5. 5
    Reveal the Button at the Off-Ramp Second

    Hide the button until the video reaches the off-ramp second from step 2. That's where the script says "click the button below this video".

    • Once shown, it stays visible.
    • Returning viewers who already passed it see it straight away.
    • Revealing it fires a vsl_cta_revealed event, so it counts as a signal too.

    On your own page, the player's time event shows the button. Most video hosts can also place a timed button inside the player.

  6. 6
    Show the Bridge Only Past the Threshold

    The bridge is the first ask: "Part 2 goes deeper. Where should we send it?" It appears only once the viewer passes the threshold in your spec. Start at 75% of Part 1.

    • First name and email; WhatsApp only with a consent box.
    • One qualifying question at most.
    • Let viewers skip it. Nothing is gated before the value.
    • Save the depth they reached on the contact.

    Tip Too early and it's a squeeze page in a costume. Too late and satisfied viewers leave without asking for more.

  7. 7
    Deliver Part 2 in Seconds

    Submitting the bridge opens the Part 2 page straight away, and sends the same link by email as a backup. Part 2 goes deeper on your method, then makes the offer:

    • Deep viewers see the application and the call.
    • Others see the self-serve, lower-ticket offer.
    • The bonus promised in beat B03 is delivered here.
    Capture Needed

    Our own Part 2 access page just after a bridge submit: the Part 2 player, the two next-step cards and the bonus (build it from the rsp-part2-access-page template on the dev server, then capture).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  8. 8
    Score the Application and Route It

    The button leads to a short application, one question per screen. There's one question for each fit rule the script says out loud in beat B29. Score it on submit:

    • Top band: the booking calendar, as step 2 of 2.
    • Middle band: the self-serve offer, or a personal reply within a day.
    • Bottom band: the long-term follow-up.

    Write the bands and the rule in your spec before launch. Never score on country, age or any protected trait.

  9. 9
    Fire an Event at Every Milestone

    Without depth events you have a page, not a funnel. Send these to your analytics and your ad pixels:

    • vsl_play, vsl_unmute
    • vsl_progress_25, _50, _75, _100
    • vsl_cta_revealed, vsl_cta_click
    • bridge_shown, form_submit, application_submit

    Each event carries the UTMs, the page variant and the cut. Export the percent each person watched into the CRM.

  10. 10
    Follow Up and Retarget by Depth

    Depth, not the clock, decides the next message. The Tantra Pro Flow runs the tiers: under 25% of Part 1 → re-engage · 25–75% → the missing-piece nudge · over 75% → the Part 2 bridge.

    Build ad audiences from the same events: played but under 50%, watched past 50% with no bridge, and bridge shown but not sent.

  11. 11
    Test the Threshold First

    Your first test is where the bridge appears, not the headline. Then test the two cuts and the button label, one at a time. Keep every threshold and variant in the spec, so the page changes without anyone editing code.

Write My VSL From the Template
Use the VSL Script Template (32 beats, three acts) to write my video sales letter. Follow every beat in order, and keep each beat's goal. Rules: never invent a number, name, logo, rating, guarantee or deadline; one metaphor, one visual, one proof and one voiced objection per teaching point; two call-to-action moments only (the early off-ramp and the close).

Return: 1) the long script, 2) the 12-minute and 6-minute cuts, 3) a cue sheet with each beat's start time and on-screen cues, 4) the caption track.

My fields:
host_name: {host_name}
company_name: {company_name}
icp_role: {icp_role}
icp_industry: {icp_industry}
dream_outcome: {desired_outcome}

mechanism_name: {mechanism_name}
offer_name: {offer_name}
call_name: {call_name}
booking_link: {booking_link}
proof_library: {proof_library}
Build My Page and Forms From the Script
From my finished VSL script, write: the Part 1 page (one-line call-out, headline from beat B01, sub-head from B05, fit bullets from B29, button label from B09), the bridge form (first name, email, WhatsApp with consent, one qualifier), and the application (one question per fit rule in B29, each with a scoring rule and three bands). Then list the events the page must fire: vsl_play, vsl_progress_25/50/75/100, vsl_cta_revealed, vsl_cta_click, bridge_shown, form_submit, application_submit.

Button reveal second: {cta_reveal_seconds}. Bridge threshold: {depth_threshold_pct}% of Part 1.
