S4 · Conversion MechanismChallenge

The Multi-Day Challenge

A paid cohort that builds something real each day, gets each day's output, and hears one offer at the end.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Sell a short cohort with a small entry price, then run every day on the same six moves: watch, fill, get, do, prove, ship. Each day's answers become a personal output delivered that day, and the ascension offer lands only on the last day, to people who have already built something. Done means a test attendee can pay, join the group, answer Day 1 live and receive their Day 1 output, and every step shows up on their contact.

Steps
15
Examples
7
Runs On
Vercel · Dodo Payments · WhatsApp · Zoom · Claude Code
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Put the Whole Cohort in One Config

    Write every day's date and start time, the registration deadline, the prices per currency and what each seat includes in one file. Every page reads it. Nobody types a date or a price into a page.

    The workshop runs three 60-minute sessions (45 minutes of teaching, 15 of Q&A), and registration closes the evening before day one. All three dates sit in the hero.

    Tip To move the cohort, change the dates in the config and nothing else.

  2. 2
    Split Free and Paid Into Two Lanes

    Give each lane its own URL, so each can be tracked and improved on its own:

    • Free lane: never shows a price; its only job is the seat.
    • Paid lane: sells the seat outright, in one card listing everything included.

    The entry price filters harder than any form field. That's why a challenge takes payment at the door.

  3. 3
    Charge in the Buyer's Currency

    Keep one price table (one row per currency) and push it to your payment tool. The page shows the visitor's currency, with a switch, and the checkout charges exactly what was shown.

    Pass the lane and the UTMs into the checkout, and send the buyer back to a thank-you page for their lane.

  4. 4
    Ask the Intake Questions Before the Group Link

    The first thank-you page plays a short video, then asks the intake survey. The answers shape the attendee's personal plan and tell you who's in the room. One question is the master fork: does a page or a person close the sale?

    Show the survey before the community link. People who join the group first rarely come back to the survey.

  5. 5
    Make the Community the Daily Hub

    Create one chat group and one announcement-only channel. Joining is the last required step of registration, because that's where the join link, the reminders and the daily prompts arrive.

    Tip Until the real invite link exists, use an obvious placeholder so the flow can still be built and tested end to end.

  6. 6
    Put Every Day in Their Calendar

    Offer one Add to Google Calendar link per day, plus a single calendar file holding every session. Reminders then go out per day, not once.

  7. 7
    Give Each Day the Same Six Moves

    In the portal, each day is one section in the same order:

    1. Watch: the live session; the recording and slides afterwards.
    2. Fill: that day's questions, during the session.
    3. Get: that day's output.
    4. Do: the day's build chapter, with its templates.
    5. Prove: the checklist.
    6. Ship: post the build for review.
  8. 8
    Open Each Day on Its Morning

    Day 1 is open from the start. Later days unlock on their morning with one switch. Before then, their chapters and checklists stay readable, but the session items show when they open.

  9. 9
    Collect Answers Live, While They Watch

    Attendees answer the day's questions in a second window during the session: one question per screen, a minimum word count, and sample answers on hand. The workshop asks 12 questions on Day 1, 6 on Day 2 and 12 on Day 3.

    Submitting is the trigger for the day's output.

  10. 10
    Generate and Deliver Each Day's Output

    This is the automation a challenge adds: the daily output loop.

    1. Answers arrive with the attendee's token.
    2. A scheduled job feeds them, with that day's template, to your AI tool.
    3. It renders a PDF and a live link.
    4. It sends both by email and WhatsApp that evening, and records output_delivered on the contact.

    In the workshop, the intake plan is already generated this way. The daily outputs and their delivery are planned (board tasks T-024, T-032 and T-033).

    Tip Write one output template per day before the cohort starts. The loop is only as good as the template.

  11. 11
    Prove Each Day With a Checklist

    Each day ends with a checklist. Every row names the tool, the time it takes, and the number that proves it's done. It ticks from the attendee's own progress.

  12. 12
    Ask Everyone to Ship Their Build

    The last move each day: post what you built in the review channel. Shipped builds are proof for the attendee, feedback from the room, and the strongest signal you have of who will buy.

  13. 13
    Offer the Upgrade at Every Lock

    Free seats see exactly what they're missing. Each paid item stays visible, marked as not in their seat, with the upgrade one click away. Before any offer, the join page covers the logistics for every day, then presents the upgrade as optional, with a clear decline.

  14. 14
    Make the Ascension Offer on the Last Day

    Only on the last day, after the recap, show what continues after the cohort: keep going alone, keep going with support, or have it done with you. Make one offer at one price, then take questions before anyone decides.

    Model two purchases separately: the entry seat and the ascension. The entry price is a filter, not the business.

  15. 15
    Pay Members to Bring the Next Cohort

    Every member gets a tagged link (utm_content=<member>-<post>). The first tagged visit is stored, carried into the checkout, and matched to verified payments, with refunds excluded. Members see only their own totals, never buyer names.

    Alumni who didn't buy stay in the community, and they are the first invite to the next cohort.

    Capture Needed

    The member referral dashboard after unlocking: per-member totals for one test cohort, with no buyer names visible.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

Plan My Challenge Days
Plan a {day_count}-day challenge for {icp_role}, ending in {offer_name}. For each day give: the theme, what they build, the live session outline ({session_minutes} minutes: teaching, then Q&A), 6 to 12 questions they answer during the session, the output generated from those answers, the checklist that proves the day is done, and what they post to ship it. The offer appears only on the last day.
Write My Daily Output Template
Write the output template for Day {day_number} of my challenge. Input: the attendee's answers to these questions: {day_questions}. Output: a one-page PDF with their answers turned into a finished artefact, plus the first task for tomorrow. Never invent facts they didn't give; mark any gap as a question for them.

S5

Stage 5 of 6

Revenue & Deal Pipeline

S5 — The Close: Offer, Booking, Payment

A booked call is not revenue. A proposal is not revenue. Money in the account is revenue, and between the offer and the money there are five places people quietly fall out. Build all five now, not after you lose someone at each.

Stage 5 is where attention becomes revenue, and every mechanism feeds the same eleven-stage pipeline: Form Filled → Eval Call Scheduled → Qualified or Unqualified → Sales Call Held → Follow-Up → Proposal Sent → Proposal Accepted → Payment Completed → Onboarding → Delivery, plus a No Show exit off the booked call. Unqualified and No Show recover people instead of losing them. Each stage is entered by an event, not by someone remembering to drag a card, and each one has an owner, a clock and a follow-up that fires on its own. Build it once in GoHighLevel or in the starter CRM; only the stages in front of Form Filled change with your mechanism.

From offer to money — what they do, what your system does, what the record says
Assets this stage needs before launch: discovery script · demo script · close script · objection battlecards · proposal template · pricing calculator · no-show recovery sequence · welcome and onboarding sequence.
Task 3.6Build the Close Assets and Wire the Booking Flow

Generated from the engine, in this order — each one blocks the next:

  1. Booking page with 3–6 qualification fields. Those fields are your Day-2 diagnostic, and they double as call prep.
  2. Confirmation + two reminders, T−24h and T−1h. A booked call with no reminders is a coin flip.
  3. Three scripts — discovery, demo, close. Plus battlecards for the two objections you hear most.
  4. Proposal template and a pricing calculator, so a proposal takes ten minutes, not an afternoon.
  5. Checkout — wallets first, card below, order summary on top, and a server-side webhook confirming the charge. Never trust the browser to tell you a payment succeeded.
  6. Welcome and onboarding sequence, triggered by that webhook. The first 48 hours after payment decide your churn.
OwnerYou · AI drafts scripts and pagesToolBooking tool · payments · CRMTime5–7 hDeliverableBooking → reminders → scripts → proposal → checkout → onboardingProofA real test purchase completes and the onboarding email arrives
◆ What changes per funnel type · the close
Webinar FunnelThe close is a booked call for high ticket, or direct checkout below roughly a thousand. Above that, a page rarely carries the objection alone.
Workshop · ChallengeTwo closes. The entry checkout on day zero — which is really a qualifier — and the ascension offer on the last day, sold to people who have already paid you once and seen the method work.
Reverse SqueezeThe close is a page, routed by engagement depth. Deep consumers see the premium branch; shallow ones see the low-ticket branch. Same page template, two prices, decided by data.
Other types: tripwire and unlock-all funnels close inside the checkout with an order bump — no second page at all · downsell funnels close on the decline, which means the second offer must exist before launch · JV funnels need the revenue split resolved at checkout, automatically, or you'll be reconciling spreadsheets for months.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

The 11-Stage Deal Pipeline

One pipeline for every mechanism: eleven stages, a No Show exit, and the event that moves each contact.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build one pipeline in your CRM: eleven stages plus a No Show exit (Unqualified is the other exit), and the fields and tags every automation keys off. Each stage gets an entry event, an owner and a clock, so nothing moves because someone remembered to drag a card. You're done when a test lead walks from Form Filled to Payment Completed and a deliberate no-show gets its tag without you touching anything.

Steps
7
Examples
2
Runs On
Cal.com · Google Calendar · Fireflies · Dodo Payments

How This Changes by Mechanism

Four event stages sit in front of Form Filled: Registered → Attended or No-Show → Replay Watched, moved by the platform's own events. Below roughly a thousand, the offer is a direct checkout, and buyers jump straight to Payment Completed.

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Create the Fields Before the Stages

    Fields first, because every stage and every automation reads them. Create these on the contact, with exactly these names:

    • Attribution: source, utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_content
    • Qualification: diagnostic_score (a number) and score_band (your band labels from Day 1)
    • Routing: mechanism (webinar, rsp or challenge), priority (P1, P2 or P3), owner, next_action_date
    • Deal: deal_value, proposal_sent_at, proposal_expires_at, lost_reason, reengage_after

    The registration page from Stage 2 already writes source, the UTMs and mechanism. Don't rename them here.

  2. 2
    Add the Tags

    Tags record what a person did. The four from Day 2 are fixed and never renamed: registered, attended, no-show, purchased.

    Add the pipeline tags next to them: call-no-show (a missed sales call, kept separate from a missed session), enquiry, ghosted, nurture, deal-lost, referral, reactivated. Stage 3 also sets replay-watched.

  3. 3
    Create the Pipeline and Its Eleven Stages

    Create one pipeline called Sales and add these columns, left to right. The numbers are the stage numbers from the source whiteboard:

    • 1 Form Filled
    • 2 Eval Call Scheduled
    • 2b No Show (exit A, hanging off stage 2)
    • 3 Qualified
    • 4 Unqualified (exit B)
    • 5 Sales Call Held
    • 6 Follow-Up
    • 7 Proposal Sent
    • 8 Proposal Accepted
    • 9 Payment Completed
    • 10 Onboarding
    • 11 Delivery

    That's eleven stages plus the No Show exit: twelve columns. One pipeline serves every mechanism. Only the stages in front of Form Filled change, and the three blocks below show exactly how.

    Tip Ten honest stages beat twenty aspirational ones. If you can't name the event that moves someone into a stage, delete the stage.

  4. 4
    Write the Trigger Next to Every Stage

    Write the entry event beside each stage before you build a single automation:

    • Form Filled: the booking or qualification form is submitted
    • Eval Call Scheduled: a calendar booking is created
    • No Show: the appointment is marked no-show
    • Qualified / Unqualified: diagnostic_score is above or below your threshold
    • Sales Call Held: the appointment is marked showed
    • Follow-Up: the closer logs "no decision" on the call
    • Proposal Sent: the proposal goes out
    • Proposal Accepted: it's e-signed or accepted in writing
    • Payment Completed: the payment webhook confirms the charge and adds purchased
    • Onboarding: the kickoff is booked
    • Delivery: the kickoff is held

    This list is automation 6 in the playbook (tag or event → stage). Stage 3 builds the others.

  5. 5
    Give Every Stage an Owner and a Clock

    Three roles cover the whole chain, even if one person plays all three:

    • Setter: owns Form Filled, enquiries and No Show. First response inside 24 hours; enquiries get a call inside 5 minutes during working hours.
    • Closer: owns the call, Follow-Up and the proposal. The proposal goes out within 24 hours of a good call.
    • Coordinator: assigns leads, fixes missing data within 6 hours, and reviews anything stuck in Follow-Up for more than 7 days.

    Set owner and next_action_date on every open deal. A deal without a next action is a deal nobody is working.

  6. 6
    Build the Two Exits

    Exit A · No Show: a missed call gets a rebook link inside the hour, then the recovery sequence. Rebooked goes back to Eval Call Scheduled; silent after 7 days is tagged ghosted and handed to the 52-week engine.

    Exit B · Unqualified: a soft let-down email, then 30 days of nurture, then back to the top. Unqualified today isn't unqualified forever.

    Both exits have their own small pipelines in The Four Extra Pipelines below.

  7. 7
    Test It With a Fake Lead

    Book a call as a test contact with a UTM on the link. Then check:

    1. The contact exists with source and the UTMs filled.
    2. It sits in Eval Call Scheduled and the confirmation arrived.
    3. Mark the appointment no-show. The call-no-show tag and the No Show stage appear without you touching them.
    4. Rebook, mark it showed, and walk it through to a test payment. The welcome email arrives.

    If any step needed your hand, that transition isn't wired yet.

    Capture Needed

    A test contact's timeline showing the automatic stage moves and tags (GoHighLevel: Contacts → contact → Activity).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

Pipeline Changes for a Webinar

Four event stages in front of Form Filled, and a checkout shortcut for lower-priced offers.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Add the event stages in front of Form Filled so you can see who registered, who joined live, who missed it and who caught the replay. Give lower-priced offers a checkout that skips the call. Everything from Eval Call Scheduled onwards stays exactly as the shared pipeline. You're done when a test registrant who misses the live session lands in No-Show, and a test buyer reaches Payment Completed without passing through stages 2–8.

Steps
3
Examples
3
Runs On
WebinarGeek · Cal.com · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add Registered, Attended, No-Show and Replay Watched

    Add four columns to the left of Form Filled. Each one moves on an event your webinar platform already sends (the WebinarGeek webhook names are shown; Zoom's are webinar.registration_created and participant_joined):

    • Registered, tag registered: new registration
    • Attended, tag attended: new live viewer
    • No-Show, tag no-show: no show (it fires after the broadcast ends)
    • Replay Watched, tag replay-watched: new replay viewer

    Stage 3 already sets these tags. Here you only map each tag to a stage. Count attendance by the platform's live-viewer event, not by minutes watched.

    Capture Needed

    The pipeline editor with Registered / Attended / No-Show / Replay Watched added before Form Filled (GoHighLevel: Opportunities → Pipelines → Edit).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Point the Offer Button at Two Doors

    The offer button, the chat link and the replay email all use one link ending in ?src=live, so every deal remembers it came from the session.

    • High-ticket offers: the link opens the booking page (Form Filled, then the shared chain).
    • Offers below roughly a thousand: it opens a checkout, and a paid order jumps straight to Payment Completed with the tag purchased.

    Anyone who answers "yes" to the discovery-call poll (field poll_4_answer) gets a personal booking message within the hour.

    Capture Needed

    A booking page or checkout opened from the offer link with ?src=live in the address bar (the reader's own tool).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Keep Session No-Shows Out of the Sales Chain

    Someone who missed the live session is tagged no-show and gets Stage 3's replay emails. Someone who misses a booked sales call is tagged call-no-show and gets this stage's recovery. They're different people with different messages. Never let one tag do both jobs.

    A contact record showing both the `no-show` (session) and `call-no-show` (sales call) tags as separate tags.

S5 · Revenue & Deal PipelineReverse Squeeze Page (VSL)

Pipeline Changes for a Reverse Squeeze Page

No date and no clock: watch depth and a score band decide the stage, and two prices share one pipeline.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Replace the event stages with depth stages: how far someone got through Part 1 decides what happens next, never the calendar. The bridge opt-in is where they become registered, Part 2 follows at once, and the application's score band routes them: top to the booked-call chain, middle to a lower-ticket checkout, bottom to long-term follow-up. You're done when the depth events land on a real test contact and each band reaches its next stage.

Steps
4
Examples
2
Runs On
Wistia · Dodo Payments
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add the Depth Stages

    Add VSL Started (event vsl_play; start the field max_depth_pct), then tag depth as they watch: depth-25, depth-50 and depth-75. Nurture follows the band, never a clock:

    • Under 25%: wrong person or wrong hook. One re-engage, then let them go.
    • 25–75%: interested but interrupted. Send the missing piece.
    • Past the Threshold (depth-75, event vsl_progress_75): show the Part 2 bridge.

    Keep the threshold in your spec. The playbook starts it at three-quarters through Part 1.

    Capture Needed

    The video host's engagement/heatmap view or the CRM contact timeline showing the depth-25/50/75 tags.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Make the Bridge Opt-In Your Registration

    There's no registration form up front. The bridge form ("Part 2 goes deeper. Where do I send it?") is where the contact gets the canonical registered tag. Submitting it delivers Part 2 at once, on a page plus a backup email. Every event carries utm_*, landing_variant and vsl_cut, so you can tell which cut and page earned the opt-in.

    Capture Needed

    The opt-in bridge form appearing over the Part 1 page past the threshold.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Route by Score Band, Not by Date

    The application writes score_band as top, middle or bottom, using the bands and rule written in your spec (no numbers here; the sources disagree on thresholds):

    • Top goes to Eval Call Scheduled, the full shared chain, with No Show and all.
    • Middle goes to a self-serve, lower-ticket checkout, straight to Payment Completed.
    • Bottom goes to long-term follow-up, the 52-week engine.

    On the premium branch the canonical tags mean the call: attended = call held, no-show = call missed, purchased = paid.

    Capture Needed

    A workflow If/Else branch splitting on the score_band field (GoHighLevel: Automation → Workflows → If/Else).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Stop the Clock

    The timed reminder engine (the playbook's automation 8) has nothing to count down to here, so switch it off for this pipeline. Nurture fires per person, on depth. Reminders still apply to booked calls on the top-band branch.

    Capture Needed

    The reminder workflow shown as paused/disabled for the RSP pipeline (GoHighLevel: Automation → Workflows → Draft/Publish toggle).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

What Is Northwind Route?

Northwind Route is Northwind’ innovation program that helps businesses quickly design and deploy AI-powered agents and copilots. It transforms CRM and operations with decision intelligence, predictive analytics, and automation, making systems more efficient and adaptive.
Built on technologies like Salesforce Agentforce, Einstein, and Data Cloud, Northwind Route ensures AI delivers real business value by improving decision-making, boosting productivity, and enhancing customer engagement at scale.
What is an AI agent marketplace?
An AI agent marketplace is a platform where organizations can explore and deploy prebuilt AI agents designed for specific business needs. These agents, powered by Agentic AI, act as intelligent assistants that automate processes, improve decision-making, and deliver measurable business outcomes

How can I learn more about AI and AI agents?
You can learn more through Northwind’s Northwind Route Innovation Lab resources, industry blogs, and webinars. Salesforce platforms like Trailhead also provide hands-on learning about Agentic AI and how autonomous agents can be applied in real business scenarios.

What business problems does Northwind Route solve?
Northwind Route addresses challenges such as inefficient workflows, slow decision-making, and limited customer engagement. With Agentic AI, it provides intelligent solutions that optimize operations, automate repetitive tasks, and enhance customer experiences.
Which industries can benefit from Northwind Route?
Industries like manufacturing, financial services, healthcare, retail, and high-tech can benefit the most. Any business that relies on CRM systems, customer service, or data-driven decision-making can gain value from Agentic AI solutions.

What technologies power Northwind Route?
Northwind Route is powered by Salesforce technologies such as Agentforce, Einstein, and Data Cloud, combined with Northwind’s expertise in building Agentic AI frameworks that deliver scalable business impact
How fast can Northwind Route deliver results?
With its incubation model, Northwind Route helps organizations move quickly from idea to implementation. Agentic AI agents can be deployed in weeks, driving faster ROI and operational efficiency.
How does Northwind Route ensure long-term success?
Northwind’s The Route Sprint ensures AI agents continuously learn and adapt. This means businesses benefit from ongoing improvements and sustainable results powered by Agentic AI.

S5 · Revenue & Deal PipelineChallenge

Pipeline Changes for a Challenge

Two closes: a paid entry before Day 1, then the ascension offer to people who already paid once.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Put registration, the paid entry, the intake and each day's attendance in front of Form Filled, so the pipeline shows who is still with you when the ascension offer lands on the last day. The entry payment is tagged entry-purchased and treated as a filter; purchased is kept for the ascension. You're done when a test buyer moves through Entry Purchased and each day on its own, and the ascension offer routes to the booked-call chain or a checkout.

Steps
3
Examples
2
Runs On
Dodo Payments · Claude Code
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Add Registered, Entry Purchased and Intake

    Add three columns in front of Form Filled:

    • Registered: tag registered, plus the field lane (free or paid) from the form.
    • Entry Purchased: tag entry-purchased, from the verified payment webhook. Its metadata carries the lane and the UTMs.
    • Intake Submitted: from the intake survey.

    Keep purchased for the ascension, so you can see who bought twice.

    Capture Needed

    The pipeline editor with Registered / Entry Purchased / Intake Submitted added before Form Filled.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Add One Stage per Day, and the Daily Loop

    For each day, add Day N Attended (tags attended-day-1 … attended-day-3, and no-show-day-N for a miss), moved by the live platform's participant-join event. Today only a Join-button click (session_join) is captured; true attendance tracking is planned.

    A challenge adds a ninth automation to the playbook's eight: survey submitted → the AI generates the day's output → PDF and link delivered (survey_submitted_day{N}, then output_delivered_day{N}). It is the product, and it is planned in our own build. Log each delivery, so a missing output shows up as a stuck stage. Someone who doesn't finish Day 2 is the early warning: chase them the same evening.

    Capture Needed

    The contact timeline showing attended-day-N and a daily output-delivered event (planned: T-024/T-032/T-033).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Make the Last Day the Close

    The ascension offer lands on the last day, sold to people who paid once and saw the method work. High-ticket offers go to apply or book a call (Form Filled, then the shared chain). Offers they can buy on the spot go straight to Ascended, tagged purchased.

    Everyone who doesn't ascend goes to Stage 6, split by how far they got:

    • attended every day → ascension follow-up
    • dropped after Day 1 or 2 → recordings and a catch-up
    • never attended → replay and the next cohort
    • entry buyers who didn't ascend → the offer for a set window, then the long-term track
    Capture Needed

    The final-day offer link opening a booking page or checkout (the reader's own tool).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Reminders and Follow-Ups for Every Stage

One sequence per stage, each with its own clock, channel and exit, generated from your survey answers.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Give every pipeline stage its own sequence: what fires automatically, what a person does, how fast, and where the contact goes if nothing happens. Generate the words from your Day 1 and Day 2 survey answers so every message sounds like you and names your offer, then load them into your CRM. You're done when every stage in your pipeline has a sequence with an exit condition, and a reply or a booking stops it.

Steps
6
Examples
11
Runs On
Google Calendar · Twilio · Gmail · Dodo Payments · Claude Code
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Put a Clock on Every Stage

    Copy this matrix into your spec. Each line is one sequence:

    • Enquiry: an acknowledgement email with the booking link and an SMS at once. A call within 5 minutes during working hours, then a call a day for 3 days (day 2 adds an SMS with three slots).
    • Form filled, no booking: reviewed within 12 hours. Qualified leads get a call to book; unreachable ones get the calendar link.
    • Call booked: confirmation email and SMS at once, then reminders 48 hours, 24 hours and 1 hour before.
    • No show: an SMS with new slots inside 5 minutes, an email inside 15, two calls the same day, then the 7-day workflow.
    • Follow-up: a recap email the same day; follow-ups weekly for high intent, every two weeks for medium.
    • Proposal sent: a follow-up at 48 hours and at 7 days, plus a call when it's opened.
    • Invoice sent: reminders 3 days before, on the due date, and 3 and 7 days late.
    • Paid: the welcome email at once, and kickoff booked within 3–7 business days.
    • Lost: a door-open email, a reason code and a re-engage date.
  2. 2
    Generate Your Templates From Your Survey

    Open your survey page and click Copy answers (or Download my answers). Open Claude Code in your workshop folder, paste the Generate Every Follow-Up prompt below, and paste your answers where it says so.

    It writes one file per stage into follow-ups/. Each file holds the email, SMS and WhatsApp versions, the send offsets and the exit condition, using your offer, your call name, your prep question and your channels. Read every file once. Anything that doesn't sound like you, tell it why, and it fixes it.

    Tip It only uses channels you ticked in the survey. No SMS consent means no SMS step, and it says so in the file.

    Capture Needed

    Claude Code running the follow-up prompt and the generated follow-ups/ folder listing (Claude desktop app → Code tab).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Build the Booked-Call Reminders First

    If you build only one sequence today, build this one: a booked call with no reminders is a coin flip. The trigger is a booking created. The steps are a confirmation email and SMS, a wait until 48 hours before, an email, a wait until 24 hours before, an email and SMS, a wait until 1 hour before, and an SMS.

    Put a reschedule link in every message. A moved call beats a no-show.

  4. 4
    Build the No-Show Recovery

    The trigger is an appointment marked no-show, which also adds call-no-show. The sequence:

    1. SMS within 5 minutes with new slots.
    2. Email within 15 minutes: what they'd have got, plus the rebook link.
    3. A task for two call attempts the same day.
    4. The 7-day email, SMS and call workflow.
    5. Day 7 with no reply adds ghosted and hands them to the 52-week engine.

    A rebooking at any point cancels the workflow.

  5. 5
    Build Proposal and Invoice Follow-Ups

    Proposal watchdog: the trigger is the stage moving to Proposal Sent. Wait 48 hours; if there's no reply, send the email. Wait until day 7, then create a call task and send an offer of a 15-minute walkthrough. On the expiry date, extend once or close it as lost (timing).

    Invoice reminders: the trigger is the invoice being sent. Remind 3 days before the due date, on it, then 3 and 7 days late. Payment moves the deal from the payment webhook, never from someone ticking a box.

  6. 6
    Make Every Sequence Stop When People Act

    Set one exit rule on every sequence: a reply, a booking or a stage change removes the contact. Nobody should get a no-show text after they've rebooked, or an invoice reminder after they've paid. Test each exit once with a test contact before you switch the sequence on.

Generate Every Follow-Up From Your Survey Answers
You are my revenue-operations writer. Using ONLY the facts in my survey answers below, write the follow-up templates for every stage of my sales pipeline.

My pipeline (11 stages + a No Show exit): Form Filled → Eval Call Scheduled (No Show exit) → Qualified / Unqualified → Sales Call Held → Follow-Up → Proposal Sent → Proposal Accepted → Payment Completed → Onboarding → Delivery.

Use these facts from my answers:
- Day 1: who I sell to, who signs and what they are measured on, the objection that kills deals, my offer sentence, my offer block (price, guarantee, what is and isn't included), my brand voice (use the 3 adjectives, avoid the 3 "not" adjectives), my mechanism and its steps, my strongest proof.
- Day 2: my funnel shape / mechanism, the missing link in my close chain, who works each stage, how my offer closes, which follow-up channels I may use, my call's name and prep question, my follow-up rules (no-show, proposal expiry, "not now"), which extra pipelines I'm running.

Write one markdown file per sequence into a folder called follow-ups/:
01-enquiry.md · 02-form-no-booking.md · 03-call-reminders.md · 04-no-show-recovery.md · 05-post-call-recap.md · 06-follow-up.md · 07-proposal-watchdog.md · 08-invoice-reminders.md · 09-welcome-onboarding.md · 10-deal-lost.md · 11-nurture-check-in.md
plus one file per extra pipeline I chose (no-show recovery, nurture-back, referral & expansion, re-engagement).

Each file must contain:
1. Trigger (the event that starts it) and exit (what stops it: a reply, a booking or a stage change).
2. A table of steps: offset (e.g. +5 min, T−24h, day 3), channel, owner (automation or which role), purpose.
3. The full copy for every step, per channel: email (subject, preheader, body), SMS (one segment: 160 characters in plain text, 70 if it contains an emoji), WhatsApp (under 400 characters; mark it "needs approved template" if it's business-initiated), and a call script of 3–5 lines for call steps.
4. Personalisation fields in {curly_braces}: {first_name}, {booking_link}, {meeting_link}, {reschedule_link}, {invoice_number}, {amount}, {due_date}, {payment_link}, {expiry_date}.

Rules:
- Only use channels I ticked. If I didn't tick SMS, write no SMS steps and say why at the top of the file.
- Use my call's name and my prep question in the booking and reminder messages.
- Use my proposal expiry and "not now" timing exactly as I wrote them.
- No invented numbers, results, testimonials or client names. If a message needs proof, use my strongest proof exactly as written, or leave {proof} as a placeholder.
- Sound like my brand voice. Short sentences. No hype words.

When you're done, print a one-line summary per file, then ask me which file I want to review first.

MY SURVEY ANSWERS:
<paste your Day 1 and Day 2 answers here>

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

The Four Extra Pipelines

No-show recovery, nurture-back, referrals and re-engagement, each ending back in the main pipeline.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build four small pipelines beside the main one, so the people it would otherwise forget are tracked like deals: missed calls, the "not now"s, happy customers who could refer, and contacts who've gone quiet. Each has its own few stages, one owner and one way back into the main pipeline. You're done when each extra pipeline has an entry trigger, a weekly review, and an exit that lands in the main pipeline or the 52-week engine.

Steps
5
Examples
7
Runs On
Gmail · GoHighLevel
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    No-Show Recovery: Missed → Rebooked or Ghosted

    Stages: Missed → Rebook Offered → Rebooked | Ghosted.

    • Enters: the tag call-no-show.
    • Runs: the recovery sequence (SMS in 5 minutes, email in 15, two calls the same day, then 7 days of mixed touches).
    • Leaves: Rebooked returns to the main pipeline at Eval Call Scheduled. Silent at day 7 is tagged ghosted and moves to the 52-week engine.

    A booked call you lose is still a warm lead.

  2. 2
    Nurture-Back: For Every "Not Now"

    Stages: Parked → Warming → Check-In Call → Back in Pipeline | Stay Parked.

    • Enters: the tag nurture, or a lost deal with the reason "timing". Set reengage_after to the date they gave you.
    • Warming: they opened or clicked something in the last 30 days, or reengage_after has arrived.
    • Check-In Call: a short, personal note or call. Quarterly at most while they stay parked.
    • Leaves: ready goes back to Form Filled or Eval Call Scheduled.

    Unqualified today isn't unqualified forever.

  3. 3
    Referral and Expansion: Ask at the High Point

    Stages: Advocate Identified → Ask Made → Intro Received → Referral Booked, with a side branch Upsell Proposed → Won.

    • Enters: a customer in Delivery gives a positive check-in or tells you about a result.
    • Ask Made: ask for one specific kind of person and offer a two-line intro they can forward.
    • Leaves: referred leads enter the main pipeline tagged referral, so you can see what advocates are worth. Expansion work is proposed to existing customers here, before you chase new ones.

    Advocates are the cheapest acquisition channel you have.

  4. 4
    Re-Engagement: The Nine-Word Email

    Stages: Dormant → Nine-Word Email Sent → Replied | Silent → Reactivated | Suppressed.

    • Enters: no opens in 90 days (or an old list you never followed up).
    • The email: a first-name subject and one plain question, e.g. "Are you still interested in {result_metric} for {company_name}?". A/B test it against an AI-personalised version that names one detail from their record.
    • Leaves: any reply is tagged reactivated and goes back to the main pipeline. Ten unopened sends means suppressed, and they drop to a lower send frequency. Let people leave quietly.
  5. 5
    Review All Four Once a Week

    Give each extra pipeline one owner and fifteen minutes a week. Look for three things: cards with no next-action date, cards that haven't moved in two weeks, and anyone who replied but was never answered. Every extra pipeline ends by handing back to the main pipeline or to the 52-week engine. None of them is a dead end.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Set It Up in GoHighLevel

Path A: fields, tags, five pipelines, the booking calendar and the workflows, all inside GoHighLevel.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build the whole of Stage 5 inside GoHighLevel: the fields and tags, the Sales pipeline with its eleven stages and No Show exit, the four extra pipelines, a booking calendar with its reminders, and the workflows that move deals and send follow-ups on their own. Paste in the copy you generated from your survey. You're done when a test contact books, misses, rebooks and pays, and every stage move and message happens without you.

Steps
9
Examples
4
Runs On
GoHighLevel · Google Calendar · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Start From a Clean Sub-Account

    Do the build in its own sub-account, so test contacts and workflows never mix with anything live. If your agency already has a pipeline snapshot you trust, open Account Snapshots in the agency view and create the sub-account from it, then check every stage and field against this guide. Otherwise start empty. It takes less time than untangling someone else's stages.

  2. 2
    Create the Custom Fields

    Go to Settings → Custom Fields, choose the Contact object and click Create field. Create each field from the fields list in The 11-Stage Deal Pipeline, with exactly those names: source, the four UTMs, mechanism (dropdown), diagnostic_score (number), score_band (dropdown), priority (dropdown P1–P3), owner, next_action_date (date).

    Then switch the object to Opportunity and create the deal fields: deal_value, proposal_sent_at, proposal_expires_at, lost_reason (dropdown), reengage_after.

  3. 3
    Create the Tags

    Tags are created the first time you type them. Open Contacts, tick your test contact, click the Add Tag icon and type each tag once: registered, attended, no-show, purchased, replay-watched, call-no-show, enquiry, ghosted, nurture, deal-lost, referral, reactivated. Spell them exactly like this; every workflow matches on the text.

  4. 4
    Build the Sales Pipeline and the Four Extra Pipelines

    Go to Opportunities → Pipelines → Create new pipeline. Name it Sales and add the stages in order: Form Filled, Eval Call Scheduled, No Show, Qualified, Unqualified, Sales Call Held, Follow-Up, Proposal Sent, Proposal Accepted, Payment Completed, Onboarding, Delivery. Use the arrows to reorder and Add stage for each one.

    Give the two exits (No Show, Unqualified) a stage colour so they stand out on the board. Then create four more pipelines the same way: No-Show Recovery, Nurture-Back, Referral and Expansion, Re-Engagement, with the stages listed in The Four Extra Pipelines.

  5. 5
    Set Up the Booking Calendar and Its Reminders

    Go to Settings → Calendars, open your sales-call calendar with Edit, then Notifications. Turn on the booking confirmation for the contact on Email and SMS, and add reminders at 48 hours, 24 hours and 1 hour before the appointment. Paste in your generated copy from follow-ups/03-call-reminders.md.

    Add your prep question as a required question on the booking form, so it lands on the contact before the call.

  6. 6
    Wire Tag to Stage

    This is automation 6: tags and events move deals, people don't. Go to Automation → Workflows → Create Workflow. Build one small workflow per move, for example:

    • Trigger: Customer Booked Appointment. Action: Create/Update Opportunity → Sales → Eval Call Scheduled.
    • Trigger: Appointment Status = Showed. Action: update the opportunity to Sales Call Held.
    • Trigger: Contact Tag added purchased. Action: update the opportunity to Payment Completed.

    Turn on Allow Opportunity to Move in the action, or the card stays where it is.

  7. 7
    Build the No-Show and Follow-Up Workflows

    One workflow per sequence in your follow-ups/ folder. For the no-show:

    1. Trigger: Appointment Status = No Show.
    2. Actions: add tag call-no-show, move to No Show, Send SMS (your 5-minute text), Wait 10 minutes, Send Email, create two call tasks, then the 7-day steps with Wait between them.
    3. Goal: Customer Booked Appointment, so a rebooking ends the workflow.

    Build the proposal watchdog the same way, with Pipeline Stage Changed → Proposal Sent as the trigger and waits of 48 hours and 7 days.

  8. 8
    Catch Deals That Stop Moving

    Add one more workflow with the Stale Opportunities trigger, filtered to the Sales pipeline, with Duration in days set to 7. The action is a task for the coordinator: "Stuck in stage: decide the next action or close it". It's the 7-day Follow-Up rule, enforced by the system instead of by memory.

  9. 9
    Walk a Test Contact Through the Board

    Open Opportunities and add a test contact through your real booking link. Watch the card: Eval Call Scheduled, then mark the appointment no-show and see it jump to No Show with the tag and the text sent. Rebook, mark it showed, move it through a proposal, and pay with a test payment. If you had to drag a card at any point, that move still needs its workflow.

S5 · Revenue & Deal Pipeline

Set It Up With the Starter CRM and Claude Code

Path B: a small CRM you run from a folder; Claude Code connects your forms, calendar, payments and messages.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Run your pipeline from a folder on your own computer instead of a subscription CRM. The starter CRM already stores contacts, records events and moves deals through the eleven stages on its own. You paste six prompts into Claude Code to connect your form, calendar, payments and messages. You're done when a real booking and a test payment move a contact through the pipeline and its follow-ups send without you.

Steps
6
Examples
3
Runs On
Cal.com · Dodo Payments · Claude Code · GitHub · Resend · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Get the Starter CRM

    Download the folder: crm-starter.zip ↗. Unzip it into your workshop folder and open a terminal there. Inside:

    • pipeline.json: the eleven stages, the No Show exit, the entry event for each, and the front stages for your mechanism
    • fields.json: the tags and fields, with the same names as every other guide
    • crm.py: the core, with no installs needed (Python 3 only)
    • prompts/: the six Claude Code prompts that connect it to your tools

    The README's status table says honestly what's built and what you build with the prompts.

  2. 2
    Walk a Test Contact Through It

    Run these one at a time:

    1. python3 crm.py init
    2. python3 crm.py add you@example.com --mechanism webinar
    3. python3 crm.py event you@example.com form.submitted
    4. python3 crm.py event you@example.com booking.created
    5. python3 crm.py event you@example.com booking.no_show
    6. python3 crm.py board

    The deal is in No Show with the call-no-show tag, and you never moved it. Tools report events; events move deals. That's the whole design.

  3. 3
    Connect Your Forms and Calendar (Prompt 01)

    Open Claude Code in the crm-starter folder and paste prompts/01-intake.md. Fill in the two tool names it asks for. Claude reads the folder, finds your tools' API docs, asks you to put each key in .env (never in the chat), and builds intake.py, which checks for new submissions and bookings every 5 minutes.

    It polls rather than waiting for webhooks, because a CRM on your own machine can't be reached from the internet.

    Tip Keys go in .env, which is already git-ignored. Never paste a key into a prompt.

    Capture Needed

    Claude Code open in crm-starter with prompt 01 pasted, reading README.md and pipeline.json.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Connect Payments (Prompt 02)

    Paste prompts/02-payments.md and name your payment provider. Claude builds payments.py, which confirms each payment with the provider's own API, never with the browser, and records payment.succeeded. The CRM adds purchased and moves the deal to Payment Completed. Prove it with one test-mode payment.

    Capture Needed

    Planned: payments.py is built by the reader with prompt 02, so there is nothing to capture until it exists. Capture crm.py show after a test-mode payment.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Start the Follow-Ups (Prompt 03)

    This one needs the follow-ups/ folder you generated in Reminders and Follow-Ups for Every Stage. Paste prompts/03-follow-up-runner.md. Claude builds runner.py, which schedules each stage's steps when a deal enters it, cancels them when the person replies, books or moves on, and sends what's due every 5 minutes by email, SMS or WhatsApp, only on channels they agreed to.

    Run python3 runner.py --dry-run and read the next 24 hours of messages before you switch real sending on.

    Capture Needed

    Planned: runner.py is built by the reader with prompt 03. Capture its --dry-run output for a test contact.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  6. 6
    Add the Extra Pipelines, a Board and a Schedule (Prompts 04–06)
    • 04 adds the four extra pipelines next to Sales.
    • 05 builds a local board at http://localhost:8765, with columns in pipeline order and one card per deal.
    • 06 makes intake, payments and the runner run every 5 minutes on their own, and writes a daily 08:00 summary of new leads, moves, sends and anything stuck.

    When all six are done, update the README's status table. Nothing in this setup depends on a third-party automation platform.

Stage 6 of 6

52-Week Growth Engine

S6 — What Happens to Everyone Who Didn't Buy

Most of your list, on any given cycle, will not buy. That is normal and it is not failure — it's timing. The mistake is letting them go quiet, because a warm list that goes silent for six months is a cold list again.

Most of your list, on any cycle, won't buy yet. Stage 6 keeps them warm for a year: one weekly email that teaches your method a step at a time and proves it with stories, a short WhatsApp message beside every email, and a rare SMS when something is time-critical. The newsletter is drafted by an AI every week from your own context and that week's news; you edit, approve and schedule it. Everyone enters through one tag, and anyone who replies re-enters the pipeline.

◆ Do this · define the four tags now and never rename them

registered · attended · no-show · purchased. Every automation, every report and every audience you build for the rest of the year keys off these four. Name them today, write them into the spec, and treat renaming one as a breaking change — because it is.

S6 · 52-Week Growth Engine

The Weekly Newsletter

A welcome series that teaches your method step by step, then a weekly letter on a 12-topic rotation.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Build the email side of the 52-week engine. Everyone who finishes without buying gets a welcome series that teaches your method one step at a time and proves it with case studies and tool how-tos, then a weekly letter on a 12-topic rotation. It lives in Beehiiv (or your email tool), enters through one tag, and sends people who reply back to the pipeline. You're done when the series is written, the automation is live, and the first weekly letter is scheduled.

Steps
7
Examples
11
Runs On
Beehiiv · GoHighLevel

How This Changes by Mechanism

The series walks through the steps you taught in the session, so Email 1 can say "you saw the overview live; here's each step in depth".

3Step by Step
  1. 1
    One Entry Tag, Four Segments

    Everyone enters through one tag, from Stage 3 or Stage 5: finished the event without buying, lost with a "not now", or ghosted. Inside the letter, keep four segments apart:

    • Non-buyers: the biggest group. Keep teaching, and re-invite them each cycle.
    • Buyers: onboarding first, then the next rung up.
    • Lapsed: one reactivation offer, then less often.
    • Advocates: ask for referrals and reviews.

    In Beehiiv, a tag per segment is enough. Create them under Audience → Subscribers → Tags.

  2. 2
    Write Email 1: The Roadmap

    The first email thanks them for coming and lists every step of your method that the series will walk through, one line each. It turns a list of emails into a course they want to finish.

    • Subject: the outcome, not the event. Preheader: the promise of the steps.
    • Body: thanks, the problem the series solves, the numbered steps, and "I'll walk you through each one in the next emails."
    • Sign-off: your first name. Rotate sign-offs across the series.
  3. 3
    Rotate Three Kinds of Email

    After Email 1, repeat this rotation until every step is covered:

    1. Step email: "(Step N/total)" in the subject. One idea, one task for the week, 4–5 questions to answer, a reply prompt, and a P.S. teasing the next step.
    2. Case study: Who? · Problem · Solution · Did it work? Then one call to book. Only results the customer approved in writing.
    3. Tool how-to: a practical walkthrough of one tool or tactic. Send a text version and a version with an image, and keep the one that gets more clicks.

    After the last step: one mindset email, then two templates they can use (an event template, an outreach template), then the weekly letter.

    Tip Write the whole series in one sitting from your mechanism's steps (Day 1). The AI newsletter guide below drafts it for you.

  4. 4
    Build the Series as a Beehiiv Automation

    Go to Audience → Automations → New automation. Pick the trigger Signed up (or Segment action if people arrive by tag from your CRM), then add an email step and a time delay for each email in the series, in order. Activate the trigger when the last email is in.

    Test the cadence for the first month: send one group daily, one every 2 days and one every 3 days, then keep the winner for everyone.

  5. 5
    Then the Weekly Letter: The 12-Topic Rotation

    Once the series ends, send one letter a week. What it's about comes from the playbook's 12-topic rotation: one theme per month, six kinds of theme, run twice a year:

    1. the problem, restated
    2. your mechanism, one step
    3. a customer story
    4. a common mistake
    5. a tool or template
    6. an invitation back in

    Every weekly letter that month goes deeper on the month's theme, and the WhatsApp and SMS twins reuse it. Keep a rough ratio of four useful sends for every one that asks for something.

  6. 6
    Let People Leave Quietly

    Remove anyone after 20 unopened emails. A list that never opens hurts delivery for the people who do. Put a visible unsubscribe and a "less often" option in every footer.

    For an old list you never followed up, run the reactivation series first: a nine-word email ("Are you still interested in {result_metric}?") A/B tested against an AI-personalised one. Anyone who opens joins the welcome series; anyone silent after 10 sends is removed.

    Capture Needed

    beehiiv segment or automation condition for unengaged subscribers.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Schedule Each Letter Into Its Slot

    Pick one day and time and never move it, so readers learn when to expect you. In the post flow, go to Review → Schedule → Schedule for later, set the date and time, and confirm. The button changes to show the scheduled time. The AI newsletter guide below drafts each letter a day or two before this slot.

Northwind

NEWSLETTER STRATEGY AND ROADMAP

Step 1 : CORE INTELLIGENCE SYNTHESIS
Key Themes and Recurring Ideas

Rising product and service complexity. The webinar script opens with this explicitly: systems today were built for a time when products had fewer variations and customer journeys were straightforward. The phone plan analogy from Daniel Reyes's script illustrates this well: ten years ago a plan was simple, one device, one price. Today it involves family plans, multiple devices, layered promotions, loyalty discounts, and bundled perks. The product improved for the customer but broke the service model underneath it.
Cognitive overload as a systemic problem. This is a central frame throughout both the deck and the script. Service reps are constantly switching between systems, deciding what applies to each customer, piecing together context. Priya Shah's Q&A adds the pre-AI version of this: a customer service agent handling 100 orders a day could not recollect the history of each account. They had to visit a fulfillment system, a ticketing system, a settlement system, and a finance system just to resolve a single case.
Automation solved the easy problems and made everything harder. The script states this directly: automation has already taken care of the easier problems, so what reaches a human rep today is almost always more complex and more emotionally charged. Priya Shah reinforces this in the Q&A by noting that people sometimes raise tickets with fabricated images generated by AI tools, or use explicit language, which requires human judgment to handle.
B2B inquiries carry unmentioned context. A recurring idea in the deck and script is that B2B customer inquiries are relationship-driven and contextual. They come from ongoing engagements. The customer does not need to explain their history because they expect the company already knows it. The challenge is surfacing that context quickly enough to respond well.
AI as practical infrastructure, not experiment. Both Daniel Reyes and Priya Shah position AI as deployable today, not in a future state. Priya Shah describes the evolution from process automation to RPA to AI and says most organisations have already made some investment in AI. Daniel Reyes's script says organisations are no longer debating AI, they are using it as a differentiator.
Human in the loop as a design principle. The B2B inquiry agent drafts an email for human approval before sending. Priya Shah explains that emotionally charged cases requiring human judgment are handed off to human agents. This is not a limitation but a deliberate architecture.
Measurable, specific KPI outcomes. The deck provides precise numbers from real deployments. These are not estimates or projections; they are reported outcomes from live clients.

Step 2 Core Problems the Company Solves

All of the following are drawn directly from the documents:
41% of customers receive different answers from different agents. Source: Forrester-based survey cited in the deck and script.
68% of customers need to put in high effort to get their problem solved. Source: Wall Street Journal survey cited in the deck and script.
20% of a service representative's working hours are spent searching for information rather than solving customer problems. Source: Salesforce survey cited in the deck and script.
Service reps must mentally stitch together information across multiple tools, rules, and exceptions, which increases cognitive load and slows resolution even for simple issues. Source: webinar script.
Field staff arrive on site with little context, spend the first ten minutes hunting for service history, and that delay snowballs into a late fix and a frustrated customer. Source: webinar script.
Service managers lose visibility and control as cases span teams, tools, and handoffs, causing delays and escalations. They cannot answer: what is the bottleneck, who is accountable for the next step, and how do we move from here. Source: webinar deck and script.
B2B customer inquiry emails contain vague product references, indirect descriptions, or customer-specific language that does not match internal system terminology, requiring a rep to decode the email, check multiple systems, and compose a response manually in 15-20 minutes. Source: webinar script.

Step 3: THE SIX CONTENT PILLARS

Every newsletter maps to one of six content pillars. These pillars ensure the year covers all dimensions of the decision-maker's evaluation journey without repetition, and that each edition has a clear editorial purpose.
Pillar 1 — Problem Illumination Reveals the service complexity crisis, cognitive overload, and broken legacy systems. Creates shared language and urgency. Buying stage: Awareness.
Pillar 2 — Agentic AI Education Demystifies Agentforce, MCP, A2A protocols, LLMs, SLMs, and AI testing. Builds technical credibility with IT and business leaders simultaneously. Buying stage: Consideration.
Pillar 3 — Use Case Proof Shows real-world deployments in B2B enquiries, field service, complex case resolution, manufacturing, healthcare, and automotive. Makes the abstract concrete and measurable. Buying stage: Consideration through Decision.
Pillar 4 — Transformation Roadmap Guides leaders from POC thinking through to scale. Addresses the "how do we actually do this?" question that stalls most AI initiatives. Buying stage: Decision through Purchase.
Pillar 5 — Industry Intelligence Shares market data, sector-specific benchmarks, and technology trends. Positions Northwind as a well-read, globally aware advisor who thinks beyond the sale. Buying stage: Awareness through Consideration.
Pillar 6 — Authority and Trust Showcases Northwind's people, credentials, philosophy, client relationships, and community. Builds the human trust that ultimately closes enterprise deals. Buying stage: All stages, trust reinforcement.

Step 4 : Key Differentiators and Unique Propositions

Drawn exclusively from the documents:
Over 20 live AI agents deployed across global customers, with 5-6 being pure customer service agents. Source: Priya Shah's Q&A.
AI-testing-AI methodology using an internal tool called ROUTE Method, which generates synthetic real-world test data, simulates end-to-end agent workflows, stress-tests edge cases, and compares agent behavior against human outcomes. Northwind reports a 50% productivity improvement in their last 3-4 months of using it. Source: webinar script.
20+ ready-to-deploy agentic solutions across education, sales, service, retail and manufacturing, healthcare, marketing, not-for-profit, and automotive verticals. Source: webinar deck.
A sponsored POC model where Northwind bears the upfront build investment. The client only pays on adoption. No cost unless the POC meets mutually agreed success metrics. Source: webinar deck.
A 4-6 week POC Phase Lifecycle: identify use cases, assess data readiness, define success KPIs, set budgetary estimates and timeline, design and build the agent, confirm value, procure license beyond foundations, then scale up. Source: webinar deck.
Deep vertical expertise demonstrated through real deployments in Australian non-profit homecare, large US-based carpet and tile manufacturing, and a two-wheeler manufacturer in India. Source: webinar script and Q&A.
MCP (Model Context Protocol) integration allowing agents to access ERP systems and external tools in a system-agnostic way, without needing to understand how the external system is built or implemented. Source: webinar script.
Agentforce-based deployment that feels familiar to Salesforce customers. Source: webinar script.

Reported Business Outcomes

From the webinar deck, exact figures:
B2B Customer Inquiry Agent: CSAT up by an average of 1.2 points. First Time Fix Rate better by 8%. Human Agent Productivity up 2.5 times. Average Handle Time and Case Resolution Time lower by 60%. Sales Velocity and Revenue Uplift increased.
Field Service Agent (Australian homecare): Missed Work Orders in a day lower by 4%. Caregiver Utilization increased. CSAT is better by 1.4 points. Appointment Compliance improved. Mean Time to Service lower by 10%.
Case Resolution Management Agent: Case Resolution Effort reduced. Reduced Management Effort. Reduced SLA Breach Rate lowered by 6%. Reduced Escalations lowered by 8%. CSAT bettered by 0.7 points.

Step 6 : Use Cases From the Documents

Use Case 1: B2B Customer Inquiries in Manufacturing. A large US-based carpet and tile manufacturer with a decade-long client relationship. They work with dealerships and design firms. Most inquiries come from existing customers checking inventory availability. The agent reads the email, identifies product names, SKUs, and indirect references, deduces actual product SKUs, pulls inventory from the ERP via MCP, recommends alternatives when products are not in stock, and drafts an email response for human approval. The script notes this saves over 10 minutes per case and makes agents approximately 300% more productive.
Use Case 2: Field Service Staff Assistance in Healthcare. A non-profit healthcare organisation in Australia delivering homecare. Caregivers are under time pressure, emotionally engaged with patients, and working in environments where empathy matters more than screens. The goal was to let caregivers focus on care, not on systems. The agent named Northwind Route provides customer and asset history, task guidance, and voice assistance. It contextualises the patient's medical history and past visit details, gives care guidance, analyzes patient EHR records, schedules next visits, blocks assets, captures voice-assisted job logs and notes back into Salesforce, and looks at caregiver schedule for cascading effects of delays.
Use Case 3: Agentic Case Resolution Management. Cases spanning multiple teams generate context fragmentation almost immediately. Updates live in different systems, ownership becomes unclear. A service manager is pulled in mid-stream and expected to answer what is happening right now and what should be done next. Northwind's Northwind Route product reads everything connected to the case including the record, internal notes, emails, escalations, and SLA signals, turns them into a clear summary, identifies which teams are involved, who last acted, who owns the next step, where handoffs have stalled, and recommends next best actions. The demo in the deck shows a live Salesforce case called "Contract Approval Request" with team progress summaries and a recommended actions section showing specific named individuals and tasks.

The Agentic AI Testing Insight

This comes directly from the script and the deck. Agentic workflows are not linear. The same task can execute in many valid ways depending on context, language, data, and user behavior. The number of possible paths grows exponentially. Traditional testing cannot keep up. Northwind built ROUTE Method to test AI with AI. It generates synthetic test data, simulates end-to-end workflows, stress-tests edge cases, and compares agent behavior against human outcomes. Testing productivity improved by at least 50% in the first 3-4 months of use.

The Technology Stack Referenced

Salesforce Agentforce as the deployment platform. MCP (Model Context Protocol) for system-agnostic ERP and external data access. Salesforce Field Service for work order management. Salesforce Data Cloud and AI Cloud (certified expertise noted in host bios). LWC and Apex development (Daniel Reyes's credentials). AimplifiAI as a referenced technology partner on Northwind Route. Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication patterns supported on the Agentforce platform.

Step 7 : YEAR-LONG NARRATIVE

The 52 newsletters tell one cohesive story across four chapters. A reader who receives every edition will feel they have gone on a complete journey from understanding the problem to being ready to act.

The Reader's Journey Across Weeks

The reader is a CXO, Head of IT, Operations Leader, CRM owner, or Digital Transformation leader. They already feel what the documents describe: service systems that were not built for the complexity of today's products, teams stretched thin, cases that fall between teams, and an AI conversation they cannot ignore but have not yet acted on with confidence.
This program meets them where they are and takes them on a deliberate journey across four phases.
Phase 1 — Awareness (Weeks 1 to 12): We name the problem precisely. We make the reader feel understood. We draw on the specific language and data from the documents: the 41% inconsistency rate, the 68% high-effort rate, the 20% wasted time figure, the cognitive overload frame, the phone plan analogy. We offer no solutions yet. We earn trust by demonstrating we understand the problem more precisely than anyone else in the reader's inbox.
Phase 2 — Understanding (Weeks 13 to 26): We introduce Agentic AI not as a technology category but as a practical capability. We walk through the three use cases from the documents in concrete detail. We explain what an agent actually does step by step, using the exact workflows from the deck. The reader finishes this phase knowing what AI agents do, not just that they exist.
Phase 3 — Conviction (Weeks 27 to 39): We earn deeper credibility by addressing the hard questions the documents surface: AI hallucination risk (Priya Shah raises this in Q&A), testing complexity (the ROUTE Method section), data readiness for deployment, the gap between a pilot and a production deployment, and how to construct an ROI case. We do not shy away from these. Naming the risks builds more trust than ignoring them.
Phase 4 — Trust and Action (Weeks 40 to 52): We present outcomes with specificity, drawing directly from the KPI data in the deck. CTAs become more direct. We invite the reader to a conversation framed around the POC lifecycle and the ROUTE Method concept that appears in the deck.

Perception to Build

By Week 52, the reader should think: This organisation has done this work in the real world. They have deployed 20-plus agents. They know where the problems come from. They speak in business outcomes rather than technology features. When I am ready to move, they are the first call I make.

How the Newsletters Stay Interconnected

Each issue opens with a brief sentence connecting it to the previous phase or issue. The three use cases from the documents are introduced progressively rather than all at once. KPI data is referenced in context as the year progresses: the 60% handle time reduction introduced in the understanding phase becomes an anchor reference in the conviction phase when building ROI frameworks. The ROUTE Method testing concept introduced in mid-year becomes a point of comparison in later issues about deployment readiness.

Step 8 : THE 52-NEWSLETTER ROADMAP
PHASE 1: AWARENESS — Weeks 1 to 12 — Naming the Problem With Precision

Week 01 Title: Why Your Customer Service Is Struggling (And It Is Not Your Team's Fault) Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The structural roots of service degradation; systems built for simpler product environments Core Takeaway: The problem is not your people. It is the system they are working inside. Key Question: What would your service look like if your systems were built for the products you sell today, not the products you sold ten years ago? Content Type: Problem framing CTA Style: Soft nurture, no commercial element
Week 02 Title: The Hidden Cost of 20% — What Your Service Reps Are Really Doing All Day Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The Salesforce survey finding that 20% of rep working hours are spent searching for information Core Takeaway: Your team is not slow. They are working in a system that was not designed to give them answers fast enough. Key Question: If you recovered 20% of each rep's working week and redirected it to solving customer problems, what would that be worth? Content Type: Data-backed insight CTA Style: Reflection prompt
Week 03 Title: Three Numbers That Should Concern Every Service Leader Pillar: Measuring What Matters Topic: The 41%, 68%, and 20% statistics from Forrester, Wall Street Journal, and Salesforce cited in the deck Core Takeaway: Service failure at scale is not random. It is systemic and measurable. Key Question: Do your current service metrics suggest you are above or below these benchmarks? Content Type: Data and industry benchmarking CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 04 Title: The Phone Plan Problem: Why Better Products Create Harder Service Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The analogy from Daniel Reyes's script about how a simple phone plan became a family plan with multiple devices, layered promotions, and bundled perks Core Takeaway: Every feature you add to delight customers adds a layer of complexity your service team must absorb. Key Question: Where in your product or service portfolio have you added customer value that also added hidden service difficulty? Content Type: Storytelling and analogy CTA Style: Reflection
Week 05 Title: How B2B Customer Inquiries Carry Context That Systems Were Never Built to Hold Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The B2B inquiry overview from the deck and script; the idea that most B2B inquiries come from existing customers who expect you to already know their history Core Takeaway: In B2B, the relationship is the product. The inquiry is rarely just about the question being asked. Key Question: How many of your inbound inquiries contain implicit context that your reps have to reconstruct manually before they can respond? Content Type: Insight CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 06 Title: When Automation Succeeds, the Remaining Problems Get Harder Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The script's observation that automation has already handled the easy problems; what reaches human reps today is more complex and more emotionally charged Core Takeaway: The cases that reach your team now are harder than they were five years ago. That is not a failure. It is the logical result of automation doing its job. Key Question: How has the average complexity of cases reaching your human reps changed over the last three years? Content Type: Escalation insight CTA Style: Reflection
Week 07 Title: The CRM Measurement Trap: Are You Tracking What Your System Cost or What It Enables? Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The distinction in the script and Q&A between CRM as a repository and CRM as an active enabler of service quality Core Takeaway: A CRM that cost a lot to implement but does not improve service velocity is an expensive liability dressed as an asset. Key Question: Can you articulate the last three measurable improvements your CRM enabled for your service team? Content Type: Reframe and myth-busting CTA Style: Reflection
Week 08 Title: A Day in the Life of a Service Rep Before AI Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: Priya Shah's Q&A description of a customer service agent handling an order dispute, visiting fulfillment, ticketing, settlement, and finance systems just to process one case Core Takeaway: Systemic inefficiency looks like individual underperformance from the outside. It rarely is. Key Question: If you shadowed one of your best service reps for a full day, how many systems would they touch before they could resolve a single case? Content Type: Scenario reconstruction CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 09 Title: Three Signals That Your CRM Is Becoming a Liability Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The client qualification parameters from the POC offer: clear business problem, available and usable data, executive sponsorship — drawn from the deck Core Takeaway: The transition from CRM asset to CRM liability is gradual, then sudden. The signals are visible long before the impact becomes undeniable. Key Question: When did someone last make a CRM decision based on what the data showed rather than what the loudest voice in the room assumed? Content Type: Diagnostic framework CTA Style: Consultative
Week 10 Title: The Manager's Blindspot: What Gets Lost Between Teams Pillar: The Complexity Problem Topic: The case resolution management overview from the deck; managers losing visibility and control as cases span teams, tools, and handoffs Core Takeaway: The biggest delays in complex cases do not happen inside a team. They happen in the space between teams. Key Question: In your most complex case type, can you map every handoff and identify exactly where context gets lost? Content Type: Problem framing CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 11 Title: Why AI Is No Longer a Pilot Program — The Competitive Reality in 2025 Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: The Why Agentic AI Today slide in the deck: models ready, productivity shift, lower cost barrier, shift happening now. Companies competing on AI adoption. Core Takeaway: Your competitors are not debating AI anymore. They are deploying it. The debate has moved from whether to how fast. Key Question: What would it mean for your service cost structure if your closest competitor achieved 2.5x service productivity this year? Content Type: Market trend and competitive context CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 12 Title: The Service Complexity Audit: A Starting Framework for Leaders Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: Synthesises the complexity frames introduced in Weeks 1-11 into a structured self-assessment, using language from the deck and script Core Takeaway: You cannot redesign a system you have not yet fully mapped. Key Question: If you had to score your service operation on rising complexity, cognitive overload, and service quality decline, what scores would you give today? Content Type: Framework and self-assessment CTA Style: Consultative inquiry

PHASE 2: UNDERSTANDING — Weeks 13 to 26 — From Problem to Possibility

Week 13 Title: What Agentic AI Actually Means — And Why the Term Matters Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The distinction the script draws between basic automation, copilots, and AI agents. Agents reason, retrieve, and act. Core Takeaway: A chatbot responds. An AI agent reasons. Understanding the difference is the first decision in any deployment. Key Question: Do your teams have a shared, precise definition of what an AI agent is and what it is not? Content Type: Educational explainer CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 14 Title: The Inquiry That Contains More Than a Question Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The B2B inquiry use case introduction from the deck and script. Customer emails that reference products indirectly, use customer-specific language, and carry relational context. Core Takeaway: The hardest part of a B2B inquiry is not finding the answer. It is understanding what the question actually is. Key Question: How many inbound inquiries to your team require clarification before your team can even begin researching an answer? Content Type: Use case introduction CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 15 Title: How an AI Agent Reads a B2B Customer Email — Step by Step Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The Agent Workflow slide from the deck: step 01 customer email received, step 02 agent identifies product names and SKUs and indirect references, step 03 agent deduces actual product SKUs, step 04 inventory pulled from ERP, step 05 alternatives recommended when products not in stock, step 06 drafts email response for human approval Core Takeaway: What takes a skilled human rep 15-20 minutes can take an agent under 60 seconds, with more contextual consistency. Key Question: What would happen to your service capacity if every incoming inquiry was pre-decoded and pre-drafted before your rep opened it? Content Type: Step-by-step process walkthrough CTA Style: Watch more or learn more
Week 16 Title: The ERP-CRM Integration Gap — Where Inventory Inquiries Break Down Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The script's explanation of using MCP to retrieve real-time ERP data; the system-agnostic protocol that lets the agent call an inventory status tool without knowing how the ERP is built Core Takeaway: The bottleneck in most inventory inquiries is not the information. It is the friction between the system that holds the question and the system that holds the answer. AI can make it the highest-return channel too. Key Question: What percentage of your service interactions contain a dormant upsell or cross-sell opportunity that your reps do not have time to surface? Week 18 Title: Why Field Service Is Not a Back-Office Problem — It Is Your Brand Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The field service overview from the deck and script. Field staff arrive on site without full context. The first ten minutes are spent reconstructing what happened before. That delay becomes a frustrated customer and a late next appointment. Core Takeaway: Every field visit is a brand moment. The preparation determines the impression. Key Question: What does your field staff know about a customer before they arrive? What do they need to know that they currently do not have? Content Type: Framing and insight CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 19 Title: AI on the Road: The Voice-Enabled Assistant for Field Service Staff Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The voice assistance capability described in both the overview slide and the agent workflow slide for field service.
