Key Question: If your field staff could access full customer history, service records, and scheduling guidance entirely by voice while their hands were busy, what would that change about their service quality? Content Type: Use case walkthrough CTA Style: Learn more
Week 20 Title: The Caregiver Story: When AI Enables Presence, Not Just Productivity Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The customer success story from the deck and script: a non-profit healthcare organisation in Australia deploying caregivers into homes. Caregivers are under time pressure, emotionally engaged with patients, working in environments where empathy matters more than screens. The goal was to let caregivers focus on care, not on systems. Core Takeaway: The highest-value outcome of AI in field service is not efficiency. It is the attention your people can give the person in front of them when systems stop demanding their attention instead. Key Question: What would change about the quality of care or service your field staff delivers if they could direct their full attention to the customer rather than the screen? Content Type: Case-style story CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 21 Title: The Living Case Summary — What It Is and Why Service Leaders Need It Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The case resolution management overview. The agent reads everything connected to the case: the record, internal notes, emails, escalations, SLA signals. It answers three questions: what has happened so far, where does the case stand right now, and what is slowing it down. Core Takeaway: A case that no one fully understands cannot be efficiently resolved. Key Question: At any moment in your most complex open case right now, can you answer: what has happened, what is stuck, and what should happen next? Content Type: Concept introduction CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 22 Title: The Service Manager's Real Job — And What Gets in the Way of Doing It Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: The script's framing of the service manager problem: they do not lack authority or experience, what they lack is clarity. Without clarity even strong leaders are forced into reactive mode. Core Takeaway: The cost of managerial firefighting is not just time. It is the decisions that did not get made while the fire was being fought. Key Question: What proportion of your week as a service leader is spent reconstructing what has already happened versus deciding what should happen next? Content Type: Leadership insight CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 23 Title: When AI Agents Collaborate: The Agent-to-Agent Architecture Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The Enquiry Agent Roadmap slide and the script's description of A2A communication. A domain orchestrator agent decomposes an email containing multiple requests, calls a specialist inventory agent and a specialist shipment status agent, coordinates their responses, and returns a single unified reply to the customer. Core Takeaway: Multi-agent systems do not just increase speed. They change what complexity is solvable at all. Key Question: If three AI agents could work on a single customer request simultaneously, what kinds of requests could your team offer to handle that you currently cannot? Content Type: Technical concept CTA Style: Learn more
Week 24 Title: From Reactive to Proactive: Redesigning Case Management Around Early Warning Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The script's description of the feedback loop created by Northwind Route: the agent tracks progress, refreshes the summary, and monitors whether the case is stabilising. If risk indicators drop, leaders can step back. If they do not, the agent flags early before the case escalates. Core Takeaway: The best service managers are not the fastest firefighters. They are the best early responders. Key Question: What risk signals exist in your current open cases right now that no one is acting on because they are buried in emails and comments? Content Type: Strategy and framework CTA Style: Consultative inquiry
Week 25 Title: The Full KPI Picture — What Actually Changes When You Deploy AI in Service Pillar: Measuring What Matters Topic: Comprehensive review of all the KPI outcomes reported in the deck: CSAT, AHT, case resolution time, MTTS, first time fix rate, SLA breach rate, escalation rate, sales velocity, caregiver utilization, appointment compliance Core Takeaway: AI impact in service is not hypothetical. It is measurable in the metrics you already own. Key Question: Which single KPI, if it improved by 20%, would have the largest downstream impact on your business? Content Type: Data and framework CTA Style: Download or consultative
Week 26 Title: Mid-Year Checkpoint: Five Questions Every Service Leader Should Be Asking Right Now Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: A synthesis of the awareness and understanding phases; draws on the diagnostic frames from the documents to create a mid-year reflection Core Takeaway: The best time to assess your current trajectory and course-correct is always now, not at year end. Key Question: Are you 26 weeks closer to your service transformation goal than you were at the start of the year? Content Type: Reflection and self-assessment CTA Style: Consultative

PHASE 3: CONVICTION — Weeks 27 to 39 — Building Justified Confidence

Week 27 Title: The Gap Between a Successful Demo and a Deployed Agent Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The ROUTE Method introduction from the webinar: building agents is only half the journey. The testing, stabilisation, and production readiness work is what most organisations underestimate. Core Takeaway: Most AI projects do not fail in the demo. They fail in the transition from proof to production. Key Question: What would need to be true about your testing approach for your next AI pilot to become a reliably deployed capability rather than a shelf project? Content Type: Practical insight CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 28 Title: Why Testing AI Is Fundamentally Different From Testing Software Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The testing challenge described in the script and deck: agentic workflows are not linear. The same task can execute in many valid ways. Context, language, data, and user behavior change outcomes. The number of possible paths grows exponentially. Core Takeaway: If your testing strategy for AI agents looks like your testing strategy for traditional software, you are leaving the most important failure modes untested. Key Question: How do you currently validate that an AI agent will behave consistently across the full range of real-world input variations it will encounter? Content Type: Technical insight CTA Style: Learn more
Week 29 Title: The Hallucination Question: What It Is, When It Matters, and How to Manage It Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: Priya Shah's Q&A answer on hallucination: an AI agent replying based on earlier questions in a session may struggle with a completely new question. It can also mistake one case history for another. He notes this is a known problem even if he has not personally encountered a severe case at a client. Core Takeaway: Hallucination is not a reason to avoid AI. It is a reason to architect carefully, test thoroughly, and keep a human in the loop on consequential outputs. Key Question: What guardrails does your current AI deployment have to prevent inconsistent or inaccurate outputs reaching your customers? Content Type: Risk and governance CTA Style: Consultative
Week 30 Title: Human in the Loop — The Design Principle That Makes AI Safe in Customer Service Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: The consistent design principle across all three Northwind use cases: the B2B inquiry agent drafts for human approval, the caregiving agent supports rather than replaces the caregiver, the case management agent recommends actions that leaders choose whether to take Core Takeaway: AI should handle speed and scale. Human judgment should handle ambiguity, emotion, and exception. Design for both. Key Question: In your current or planned AI deployment, who reviews what, when, and why — and is that documented as part of the design? Content Type: Ethics and framework CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 31 Title: Salesforce Agentforce — What It Is, What It Is Not, and Where the Real Work Happens Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The script's explanation of Agentforce as the deployment platform; prompts and instructions wired carefully into Agentforce actions; the distinction between platform capability and the workflow design that creates actual value Core Takeaway: Platform capability is a starting point. The prompts, actions, and integrations you build on top of it are where value is actually created or lost. Key Question: How much of your current Salesforce capability is fully configured to serve your most demanding service workflows? Content Type: Educational and positioning CTA Style: Learn more
Week 32 Title: MCP — The Protocol Quietly Changing How AI Accesses Enterprise Data Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The script's specific explanation of MCP: Model Context Protocol. It lets an agent call an inventory status tool in the ERP without knowing how the ERP is built or implemented. It simply invokes the tool, retrieves the data, and continues the workflow. Core Takeaway: System-agnostic data access is what makes AI agents practically deployable in complex enterprise environments. Key Question: How many data sources would your AI agents need to access, and what would the integration architecture look like without a protocol like MCP? Content Type: Technical deep dive CTA Style: Consultative
Week 33 Title: The Carpet Manufacturer Story — 300% Productivity and Sales Through Service Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The full B2B inquiry case study from the script and deck: the large US-based carpet and tile manufacturer with a decade-long Northwind partnership; the inventory inquiry workflow; the recommendation layer; the KPI outcomes including 2.5x productivity, 60% handle time reduction, CSAT improvement, and sales velocity uplift Core Takeaway: Context-aware AI changes service from reactive lookup to proactive guidance — and the impact shows up in both service metrics and revenue metrics simultaneously. Key Question: How much revenue is your organisation leaving on the table through slow, incomplete, or inconsistent inventory responses to your key accounts? Content Type: Case-style story with KPIs CTA Style: Learn more
Week 34 Title: What 20 Deployments Teach You About Agent Design Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: Priya Shah's Q&A account of 20-plus deployed agents across global clients; 5-6 pure customer service; the range of contexts from doctor appointment booking to inventory management to bike manufacturer sales enablement; the three solutions built for the two-wheeler manufacturer in India Core Takeaway: The agents that work in production share three characteristics: focused scope, clean underlying data, and clearly defined escalation paths. Key Question: If you were to deploy a scoped AI agent in the next 90 days, what is the single most contained, high-volume problem it could address? Content Type: Lessons learned CTA Style: Consultative
Week 35 Title: Data Readiness — What AI Actually Needs From Your CRM Before You Deploy Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The client qualification parameters from the POC offer slide: available and usable data is an explicit requirement. Priya Shah's description of inventory agents needing clean bill-of-material data matched against PO requirements across multiple warehouses. Core Takeaway: Poor data does not slow AI deployment. It poisons it. Key Question: If an AI agent were to read your CRM and connected system data right now, what would it find? Content Type: Framework and practical guidance CTA Style: Assessment offer
Week 36 Title: Redesigning the Case Lifecycle — Where AI Fits and Where It Does Not Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The full case resolution management workflow from the script: what has happened, what is stuck, who owns the next step, recommended actions with named individuals, one-click task creation Core Takeaway: AI is not a bolt-on to an existing process. It works best when the process is intentionally redesigned around the points where it adds the most value. Key Question: If you mapped your most complex case type end to end, where would you place AI? Where would you keep human judgment exclusively? Content Type: Process redesign and framework CTA Style: Consultative
Week 37 Title: Why Industry Context Is Not Optional in AI Agent Design Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: Priya Shah's Q&A accounts of the differences between healthcare agents, manufacturing inventory agents, bike manufacturer sales enablement agents, and the non-profit homecare Northwind Route. Each has fundamentally different data, vocabulary, and workflow requirements. Core Takeaway: A generic AI agent is not a starting point. It is a waste of time. Industry context is not a customisation layer — it is the foundation. Key Question: Is your AI deployment strategy built for the specific workflows, data structures, and customer expectations of your industry? Content Type: Insight and positioning CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 38 Title: Building the Business Case — How to Talk to Your CFO About AI in Service Pillar: Measuring What Matters Topic: The KPI data from the deck combined with the POC offer's framing: no cost unless the POC sign-off meets mutually agreed success metrics. Using the KPIs you already measure — CSAT, SLA breach, handle time, escalation rate — as the evidence base. Core Takeaway: A credible ROI case for AI is built on the metrics you already track. You do not need a new framework. You need to apply an honest one. Key Question: Could you present a credible ROI case for AI investment to your CFO today using only your current service metrics? Content Type: Framework and how-to CTA Style: Download or consultative
Week 39 Title: The Three Mistakes That Sink AI Deployments Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: Drawing from the testing section of the script and deck, and Priya Shah's broader commentary on what goes wrong: over-scoping, under-testing, and ignoring the change management requirement Core Takeaway: The organisations that fail at AI typically deploy too broadly, too quickly, with too little preparation and no serious plan for the human side of the change. Key Question: Which of these three failure patterns is your current AI strategy most at risk of? Content Type: Lessons learned and myth-busting CTA Style: Consultative

PHASE 4: TRUST AND ACTION — Weeks 40 to 52 — From Evidence to Invitation

Week 40 Title: The Numbers That Moved — Real KPI Outcomes From Real Service Deployments Pillar: Measuring What Matters Topic: Comprehensive presentation of all three KPI wheels from the deck: B2B inquiry agent (CSAT +1.2, AHT -60%, productivity 2.5x, first time fix rate +8%, sales velocity up), field service agent (CSAT +1.4, MTTS -10%, missed work orders -4%, appointment compliance up), case management agent (CSAT +0.7, escalations -8%, SLA breach -6%, management effort reduced) Core Takeaway: These numbers are not projections or estimates. They are outcomes from live deployments with real clients. Key Question: What would a 60% reduction in case resolution time mean for your service cost structure and your customer satisfaction scores simultaneously? Content Type: Evidence and data CTA Style: Consultative
Week 41 Title: The Hardest Part of Any Transformation Is Not the Technology Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: The change management dimension implicit throughout the documents; Priya Shah's comment that caregivers' satisfaction improved not because the job became easier but because the friction around the job was removed; the script's note that documentation became more consistent and compliant because context was no longer lost between visits Core Takeaway: Technology rarely fails in transformation programs. People and process almost always do. Key Question: What change management support is built into your current AI or CRM deployment plan? Content Type: Leadership and framework CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 42 Title: What Makes a CRM Agent-Ready Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The data readiness requirement from the POC offer, combined with the script's MCP discussion and the client qualification parameters: available and usable data, existing Salesforce licenses, readiness to engage within 4-6 weeks Core Takeaway: AI does not rescue a poorly configured CRM. It amplifies whatever it finds — including the problems. Key Question: On a scale of one to ten, how agent-ready is your current CRM implementation, and what is the single biggest gap? Content Type: Framework and assessment CTA Style: Assessment offer
Week 43 Title: What a Good Proof of Concept Actually Proves Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: The POC Phase Lifecycle slide and the Agentforce POC offer from the deck: 1 POC per organisation, in a customer sandbox with limited data, sector-aligned use case, Northwind bears upfront build investment, no cost unless POC sign-off as per mutually agreed success metrics Core Takeaway: A POC that proves technical function is not enough. A good POC proves business value against the metrics that matter. Key Question: What specific measurable outcome would your next POC need to demonstrate to earn executive sponsorship for full deployment? Content Type: Strategic guidance CTA Style: POC offer
Week 44 Title: The 4-6 Week Path — From Problem Identification to Deployed Agent Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The POC Phase Lifecycle: start by assessing data readiness, identify use cases, define success KPIs, set budgetary estimates and timeline, design and build the agent, confirm value, procure license beyond foundations, scale up Core Takeaway: The distance between identifying a problem and having a working agent in front of your team is much shorter than most organisations believe. Key Question: If you started a scoped AI deployment today, what would be live and measurable in six weeks? Content Type: Process and timeline CTA Style: Book a call
Week 45 Title: AI as a Long-Term Advantage — What Compounding Capability Actually Looks Like Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: Priya Shah's commentary on the evolution from automation to RPA to narrow AI to AGI. The idea that most organisations have made initial AI investments and the question now is how to build on them strategically. Core Takeaway: AI advantage is not a one-time deployment. It builds and compounds with every case, every correction, every new workflow added. Key Question: What would your service capability look like if your AI system had two years of your operational data and case outcomes to learn from? Content Type: Strategic vision CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 46 Title: What AI Gives Your Best People Back Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: The Northwind Route story's core outcome: less distracted, reduced fatigue, more time and attention for patients. The B2B inquiry agent story's core outcome: agent can focus on relationship and judgment rather than manual lookup. The 2.5x productivity figure. Core Takeaway: The strongest argument for AI in service is not the cost reduction. It is what your best people can do when AI handles the work that was preventing them from doing it. Key Question: What are your highest-performing service reps spending time on right now that an AI agent could handle instead? Content Type: Human impact CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 47 Title: Building Agents That Know Your Industry — The Vertical Intelligence Advantage Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: The 20+ ready-to-go agentic solutions slide from the deck: solutions for education, sales, service, retail and manufacturing, marketing, not-for-profit, automotive, healthcare. Each is industry-aligned. Core Takeaway: A general-purpose agent trained on generic scenarios will underperform an industry-tuned agent trained on your operational context. Key Question: What industry-specific knowledge would your ideal AI agent need in order to be genuinely useful rather than merely functional? Content Type: Educational and positioning CTA Style: Consultative
Week 48 Title: From System of Record to System of Action — The Future of CRM Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: Priya Shah's commentary on the evolution of CRM: it used to record what happened; AI now enables it to determine what should happen next. The script's vision of the enquiry agent roadmap progressing from a single-task agent to a coordinated multi-agent system. Core Takeaway: The CRM of the next decade will not wait to be asked. It will anticipate, suggest, and act. Key Question: Is your CRM currently telling you what to do next, or only recording what you already did? Content Type: Trend and vision CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 49 Title: From One Agent to Many — The Multi-Agent Orchestration Opportunity Pillar: Technology Architecture and Integration Topic: The Enquiry Agent Roadmap slide and the script's description of agent-to-agent communication: a domain orchestrator agent decomposes complex multi-intent customer emails, calls specialist agents, coordinates responses, and composes a unified reply Core Takeaway: Single-agent deployments are the beginning. Multi-agent orchestration is where the real leverage exists. Key Question: What would a coordinated network of AI agents, each specialised for a different domain, make possible for your customer service operation? Content Type: Technical vision and strategy CTA Style: Consultative
Week 50 Title: What 20-Plus Deployments Have Taught Us About What Actually Works Pillar: Agentic AI in Practice Topic: Synthesis of all deployment insights from Priya Shah's Q&A and the script: the patterns from manufacturing, healthcare, non-profit, education, automotive, financial services contexts; what succeeded, what required redesign, what surprised the team Core Takeaway: The organisations with the deepest AI advantage are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones who learned fastest from each deployment. Key Question: What is one thing you have learned from your most recent technology deployment that you would apply differently next time? Content Type: Thought leadership and evidence CTA Style: Consultative
Week 51 Title: How Service Leaders Are Thinking Differently About AI Now Pillar: Leadership and the Human Factor Topic: Reflects on the year-long journey through the four phases; draws on the shift Priya Shah describes from automation-thinking to AI-thinking to AGI-thinking; the competitive reality framed in the Why Agentic AI Today slide Core Takeaway: The question in service leadership is no longer whether to adopt AI. It is how fast to move and what to build first. Key Question: How has your thinking about AI in customer service changed over the course of this year? Content Type: Reflective thought leadership CTA Style: Soft nurture
Week 52 Title: Your Service Transformation Roadmap — What Year Two Should Look Like Pillar: CRM Strategy and Transformation Topic: Closing synthesis drawing on the ROUTE Method concept from the deck, the POC lifecycle, and the full arc of the year; frames next steps in concrete operational terms Core Takeaway: Transformation is not an event. It is a continuous cycle of deliberate improvement built on what the previous cycle taught you. Key Question: What is the single next decision that would move your service transformation forward the most, and what is preventing you from making it? Content Type: Synthesis and action roadmap CTA Style: Book a strategy call

Hi Sam,

Thank you for joining the Masterclass on Reducing Databricks costs. I hope
you walked away with at least one thing you could go and check on Monday.

We built that session around a problem almost every data leader recognises
but very few can prove: the bill is going up faster than the value, and
nobody in the room can point at the line that's causing it.

The 8-step Databricks cost framework — Assessment, Migration, Monitoring

Over the next few weeks I'm going to walk you through the entire framework
we use on client engagements. Not the summary version. The actual steps,
with the actual read-only SQL we run.

Here's what's coming:

1. Set a baseline you can defend — every DBU with a dollar attached to it.

2. Find the idle money — the clusters billing at full rate at 2% CPU.

3. Measure the always-on tax — interactive compute doing scheduled work.

4. Quantify burn and markup — failed runs, and Photon where it wins nothing.

5. Sort every workload — Keep, Refactor, Retire, or Move to lower cost.

6. Migrate in waves and prove parity before you cut over.

7. Stand up a control tower so the savings don't quietly decay.

8. Prove the business case with numbers a CFO will accept.

Steps 1 to 4 you can run yourself this month. We publish the exact queries.
Steps 5 to 8 are where most teams want a second pair of hands, and I'll be
honest with you about which is which as we go.

One thing worth saying up front: the goal here isn't a smaller invoice. It's
getting the projects your commit is currently blocking back onto the roadmap.
The savings are how you pay for them.

Stay tuned!

Maya
Founder & CEO, Northwind

S6 · 52-Week Growth Engine

The WhatsApp Twin of Every Email

One short WhatsApp beside each email: a nudge to open it, or the same idea in a few lines.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Give every newsletter email a WhatsApp twin: either a pointer that makes the reader open the email, or the same idea in a few lines. Twins go only to people who opted in to WhatsApp, as approved message templates, an hour after the email. You're done when your first two twins are approved as templates and scheduled next to their emails.

Steps
5
Examples
2
Runs On
Beehiiv · WhatsApp · WATI
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Choose Pointer or Compressed

    Decide per email:

    • Pointer: for long emails (step emails, tool how-tos). Their name, the hook from the subject, one line of the takeaway, and the link to the email's web version.
    • Compressed: for short emails (mindset, case studies). The one idea in 3–5 lines, ending with a question they can answer by replying.

    Either way it's one idea and one link. WhatsApp is read on a phone between other things.

    Capture Needed

    A pointer twin and a compressed twin side by side in a WhatsApp chat on a phone (the reader's own WhatsApp Business account).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Stay Inside WhatsApp's Limits

    The rules come from Meta's WhatsApp Business Platform:

    • Opt-in first. You may only message people who agreed to hear from you on WhatsApp. Add the tick box to your registration form.
    • Templates outside 24 hours. A message you start (not a reply) must be an approved template. Newsletter twins are the Marketing category.
    • Length. A template body can be up to 1,024 characters. Aim for under 400: a twin is a nudge, not a copy of the email.
    • Replies. When someone replies, a 24-hour window opens and you can answer freely, up to 4,096 characters per message.

    Sources: Meta: template components ↗ · Meta: getting opt-in ↗.

    Capture Needed

    WhatsApp Manager's template category notice.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Turn Each Twin Into a Template

    Write the twin with variables for the parts that change, {{1}} for the first name and {{2}} for the link, then submit it in WhatsApp Manager (or your provider's template screen). Meta checks the category. If it says the template will be marked as marketing, that's correct for a newsletter twin: submit it.

    Make the pointer version reusable, so one approved template covers every week and only the variables change.

  4. 4
    Send It an Hour After the Email

    Schedule the twin an hour after the email lands, never at the same minute, so the WhatsApp reminds them rather than competes. Use your WhatsApp Business provider's broadcast or campaign screen, or the follow-up runner from the starter CRM (it only sends to contacts with WhatsApp consent). Replies come to a real person and count as engagement in your CRM.

    Capture Needed

    A WhatsApp Business provider's broadcast/campaign scheduling screen with a send time set (the reader's own provider).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  5. 5
    Generate the Twins With the Newsletter

    You don't write twins by hand. The AI newsletter's weekly task drafts the email and its WhatsApp twin together, checks the twin is under 400 characters, and marks which mode it used. You review both in the same place.

Write the WhatsApp Twin for an Email
Here is this week's newsletter email. Write its WhatsApp twin.

Rules:
- Choose POINTER if the email is over 250 words, otherwise COMPRESSED, and say which you chose.
- POINTER: line 1 = "Hi {{1}}," + the hook from the subject; line 2 = the one-line takeaway; line 3 = "Full thing in your inbox, or here: {{2}}".
- COMPRESSED: the single idea in 3–5 short lines, ending with a question they can answer by replying.
- Under 400 characters total (the hard limit for a template body is 1,024). Print the character count.
- My brand voice: <your three adjectives from Day 1>. No hype words, no more than one emoji.
- It will be sent as an approved Marketing template to people who opted in, an hour after the email.

EMAIL:
<paste the email>

S6 · 52-Week Growth Engine

The SMS Nudge

A one-segment text beside the emails that matter: invitations, deadlines and re-invites only.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Add an SMS to the weeks that are time-critical (doors opening, a deadline, a live session), never to every letter. Each text is one segment, which is 160 characters of plain text or 70 once there's an emoji, and goes only to people who gave SMS consent. You're done when you have a pointer text and an invitation text ready, both under one segment, and your sender is set up.

Steps
4
Examples
1
Runs On
Beehiiv · Twilio
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Decide Which Weeks Get a Text

    SMS is the rare rail. The playbook's cadence is email weekly, messaging fortnightly, and SMS only when it's time-critical. Text when:

    • a new cohort or event opens, or a seat deadline is close
    • a live session starts today
    • the "invitation back in" month of the rotation lands

    Every other week: no text. That's what keeps the texts that matter from being ignored.

    Capture Needed

    A content calendar with the SMS weeks marked (the reader's 52-week plan).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Fit It in One Segment

    A text over one segment is split and billed as several. The sizes, from Twilio's docs:

    • Plain text (GSM-7): 160 characters in one segment, 153 per segment once it splits.
    • Any emoji or non-GSM character (UCS-2): 70 in one segment, 67 per segment once it splits.

    One curly apostrophe can switch a whole text to the 70-character limit, so use straight quotes and no emoji. Source: Twilio: what is the SMS character limit? ↗

    Capture Needed

    An SMS composer showing the live character/segment counter (the reader's SMS provider).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Write the Two Texts You Need
    • Pointer: {brand}: new playbook on {topic} is in your inbox. 2-min read: {short_link}
    • Invitation: {brand}: {first_name}, doors open for {event_title} on {date}. Your seat: {short_link}. Reply STOP to opt out

    Start with who it's from, because people don't save your number. Use a short link. Include the opt-out wording where your country requires it.

    Capture Needed

    A drafted SMS in the provider's composer, with merge fields.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  4. 4
    Send Only With Consent

    Only text people who ticked SMS consent on your form. In the starter CRM that's consent_sms, and the follow-up runner refuses to text anyone without it. In GoHighLevel, use a workflow Send SMS step filtered to contacts with your SMS-consent tag. Send in their daytime, an hour after the email.

Write the SMS for This Week
Here is this week's newsletter email and what's time-critical this week: <doors opening / deadline / live session / nothing>.

If nothing is time-critical, reply "No SMS this week" and stop.
Otherwise write ONE text:
- Starts with "<brand>:" so they know who it's from.
- One reason to act now, and the {short_link}.
- Plain GSM-7 characters only: straight quotes, no emoji, no em dashes.
- 160 characters maximum INCLUDING "Reply STOP to opt out" if my country needs it (<country>).
- Print the character count and confirm it's one segment.

EMAIL:
<paste the email>

S6 · 52-Week Growth Engine

The AI Newsletter: A Weekly Draft in Your Claude Code

Run one prompt once; every week Claude Code drafts your letter from your context and the news.

1The Full Setup
2The Task

Run one prompt in Claude Code, once, with your survey answers and a few inputs. It builds a folder holding everything it knows about your business and voice, writes your first draft on the spot, and creates a weekly task that drafts the next issue from that folder and the week's news in your field. Each week you give feedback, it revises and remembers the lesson, and you schedule the result in Beehiiv. You're done when the first draft is approved and scheduled, and the weekly task shows as active.

Steps
8
Examples
4
Runs On
Claude Code · Beehiiv
3Step by Step
  1. 1
    Open Claude Code in a New Folder

    Make a folder for the letter, e.g. weekly-letter. In the Claude desktop app, open the Code tab and start a session with that folder as the working folder. The desktop app matters: its scheduled tasks run on your computer with access to your files. Tasks created in the cloud can't see a local folder.

    Claude Code in a terminal works too: open the folder in a terminal and run claude. The setup prompt handles both.

    Capture Needed

    Claude desktop app → Code tab → new session with the weekly-letter folder selected as working folder.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  2. 2
    Paste the Setup Prompt With Your Inputs

    Copy Set Up My AI Newsletter below. Fill in the inputs at the top:

    • the name
    • your send slot and a draft day one or two days earlier
    • the 3–5 topics you own and three sources you trust (your last survey answer has all of these)
    • whether your Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API
    • whether to install the schedule now

    Then paste your answers from the survey's Copy answers button and send it.

    Capture Needed

    The setup prompt pasted into a Claude Code session with the inputs filled in.

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  3. 3
    Check the Folder It Built

    It writes everything as plain files you can read and edit:

    • context/: your offer, audience, positioning and mechanism, quoted from your answers, with TODO wherever you left a gap
    • style.md: your voice, sign-offs and banned words
    • rotation.md: twelve monthly themes from your topics
    • sources.md: where the news comes from
    • feedback.md: empty until your first edit
    • weekly-task.md: the instructions the schedule runs

    Fix any TODO now. The drafts are only as good as this folder.

  4. 4
    Read Your First Draft

    Before any schedule exists, it drafts this week's issue so you can judge it. You get a file in drafts/ with:

    • three subject lines and a preheader
    • the email: a hook from this week's news, the month's theme, one thing to do this week, and a reply question
    • the WhatsApp twin, with its character count
    • an SMS twin only if something is time-critical
    • every news item with its link

    There's also an HTML version ready for Beehiiv.

  5. 5
    Give Feedback and Let It Learn

    Reply in the same session in plain words: "Too long; cut the second news item; open with the mistake, not the news." It revises the draft and adds one line per lesson to feedback.md. Every future draft reads that file first, so the second week needs fewer edits than the first.

  6. 6
    Find the Weekly Task Under Routines

    If you said yes to installing the schedule, the desktop app now has a Weekly local task. In the Code tab, click Routines in the sidebar and open it. From its page you can:

    • Run now
    • switch Status between Active and Paused
    • Edit the day, time or instructions
    • Review history

    Each run appears as a new session under Scheduled in the sidebar, with a desktop notification.

    Click Run now once and choose "always allow" for the web search and file tools it asks for, so future runs don't stall waiting for you.

    Tip Tasks only run while the app is open and the computer is awake. Turn on Keep computer awake under Settings → Desktop app → General. A missed run catches up once when the computer wakes.

    Capture Needed

    Claude desktop app → Code tab → Routines → the weekly-letter task's detail page (Run now, Status, Edit, Review history).

    A real screenshot goes here. Until then, follow the words above.

  7. 7
    Paste Into Beehiiv and Schedule It

    When you're happy, open Beehiiv, start a new post and paste the draft's HTML into the editor. Use the subject line you chose and the preheader. Then go to Review → Schedule → Schedule for later, pick your send slot and confirm. Say "sent" in the session, and the draft moves to sent/ so next week's issue builds on it.

  8. 8
    Optional: Let It Create the Beehiiv Draft

    On Beehiiv's Max and Enterprise plans, the Create Post API can put the draft straight into Beehiiv. Create an API key under Settings → Workspace Settings → API (you need to be an owner or admin), save it in the folder's .env file (never in the chat), and say "push". It creates the post as a draft. You still review it and schedule it yourself. On other plans, keep pasting: it takes a minute.

Set Up My AI Newsletter
You are setting up my AI newsletter. Do everything below in this folder, then stop and show me the first draft.

MY INPUTS
- Newsletter name: <name>
- Send slot: <day and time, with timezone>, e.g. Tuesday 09:00 America/New_York
- Draft day: one or two days before the send slot, e.g. Sunday 17:00
- Topics I own (3–5): <topics>
- News sources I trust (3): <sources: sites, newsletters, vendors' changelogs>
- Where the letter lives: Beehiiv
- My Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API (Max or Enterprise): <yes | no>
- Install the weekly schedule now: <yes | no>
- My survey answers (Day 1 and Day 2, pasted from the survey's Copy answers button):
<paste>
- One past email I liked (optional, for the voice):
<paste or "none">

1 · BUILD THE FOLDER
Create newsletter/ with:
- context/offer.md, context/audience.md, context/positioning.md, context/mechanism.md: each written ONLY from my survey answers (who I sell to and who signs, the objection, my offer sentence and offer block, my brand voice, my mechanism and its steps, my strongest proof, my chosen conversion mechanism). Quote my words; invent nothing. Mark anything missing as TODO.
- style.md: my voice (my three adjectives and my three "nots"), sentence length, sign-offs to rotate ("Stay tuned", "Stay curious, stay inspired", "Let's make waves", or ones that fit my voice), banned words (hype, "webinar" if I sell a workshop), and the rule "never state a number or a news fact without a link".
- rotation.md: the 12-month topic rotation. One theme per month, six kinds of theme run twice a year: the problem restated · my mechanism, one step · a customer story · a common mistake · a tool or template · an invitation back in. Fill each month with a theme from MY topics. Mark which month we're in now.
- sources.md: my three sources plus the search queries you'll use each week.
- feedback.md: empty, with a heading "Lessons from my edits".
- drafts/ and sent/ (empty).
- weekly-task.md: the weekly instructions (step 3 below), written out in full so the task is self-contained.

2 · WRITE THE FIRST DRAFT NOW
Follow weekly-task.md once, right now, so I can see a real draft before any schedule exists.

3 · THE WEEKLY TASK (write this into weekly-task.md)
Every week:
a. Read context/, style.md, rotation.md, feedback.md and the last 4 files in sent/.
b. Find this week's news: search the web and my sources for the last 7 days on my topics. Keep the 3 items that matter most to MY audience. Record title, date and link for each. Skip anything you can't link.
c. Pick this month's theme from rotation.md. The letter goes one level deeper on it than last week's issue in sent/.
d. Draft into drafts/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md:
   - 3 subject lines + 1 preheader
   - the email (350–600 words): a hook from this week's news → the theme → one thing to do this week → a reply question; one call to action only if this month's theme is "an invitation back in"
   - a WhatsApp twin under 400 characters (POINTER if the email is over 250 words, otherwise COMPRESSED), with its character count
   - an SMS twin ONLY if something is time-critical this week (one segment: 160 plain GSM-7 characters, no emoji), with its character count; otherwise write "No SMS this week"
   - Sources: every news item with its link
   Also write drafts/<YYYY-MM-DD>.html: the email body as clean HTML for pasting into Beehiiv.
e. Check the draft against style.md and feedback.md before finishing. List any claim without a link and remove it.
f. End with a 3-line summary: the theme, the subject you'd pick, and what you'd like my feedback on.
g. Never publish, send or schedule anything. I approve every issue.
h. When I reply with feedback in this session: revise the draft, then append one line per lesson to feedback.md ("- <date>: <what to do differently next time>").
i. When I say "sent", move the final draft to sent/. If my Beehiiv plan has the Create Post API and I say "push", create the post as a DRAFT through the API using the key in .env (never print it); otherwise tell me to paste the HTML into the Beehiiv editor.

4 · SCHEDULE IT (only if I said yes above)
- If you can create scheduled tasks here (the Claude desktop app): create a WEEKLY local scheduled task named "weekly-letter" on my draft day and time, with this folder as its working folder and the contents of weekly-task.md as its instructions.
- Otherwise (Claude Code in a terminal): write run-weekly.sh that runs `claude -p "$(cat weekly-task.md)"` in this folder and saves the output to drafts/<date>-run.log. Then install it as a weekly launchd job on my draft day and time (a cron line on Linux), and show me how to check it and how to remove it.
Then tell me exactly where to find the task and how to run it now.

Day 3Launch the AI RevOps Engine · Test It, Then Grow It

Make an AI Run the Whole Thing — Then Prove It Works

Today the funnel stops being a stack of files and becomes a living system: built by an agent, instrumented end to end, wired into a CRM and a set of automations, and then pointed at a small amount of real traffic to find out whether any of it is true.

We'll use Claude Code as the worked example throughout. The system is AI-agnostic — the same context and the same prompts work in any agentic coding tool. What matters is the ritual, not the vendor.

Step 1 — The Build Ritual

Here's the deal: the difference between an AI that builds you a funnel and an AI that builds you a generic template is what you give it before you ask. Handing an agent "build me a funnel" gets you a template. Handing it your conversion engine, your spec outline and a build checklist gets you your funnel.

Eight phases — and the agent refuses to skip ahead
Phase 3 is the whole trick. An agent that restates your spec before building gives you one cheap chance to catch a misunderstanding. An agent that starts coding immediately gives you an expensive one, later.
◆ Do this · make the agent interview you

Your first message should forbid code. Load the context, then say: "Read these in full. Confirm you've read them. Then interview me — brand and story, the diagnostic, offer and pricing, traffic channels, tech and deploy target — a few questions at a time, and wait for my answers. Restate the complete spec for my approval. Do not write any code until I approve it."

It feels slower. It is dramatically faster, because you are not debugging a funnel built on a guess.

Task 4.1Run the Ritual End to End
  1. Put your Day-2 engine, your spec outline and your Day-3 asset list in one folder.
  2. Open your agent in that folder so it can read them.
  3. Send the no-code-yet prompt. Answer the interview honestly — "I don't know yet" is a valid answer and better than a made-up one.
  4. Read the spec it restates. Actually read it. This is the cheapest review you will ever do.
  5. Approve, then let it build, showing you each stage as it lands.
OwnerYou · agent buildsToolClaude Code, or any agentic toolTime3–5 hDeliverableA live URL and a spec file you can editProofYou change a price in the spec and the live page updates

What the Orchestrator Actually Is

Once it's built, the agent doesn't go away. It keeps the context — your offer, your ICP, your pages, your templates, your numbers — and becomes the thing you and your team ask questions of and give instructions to.

The RevOps orchestrator — context in, operations out
The retention unlock: a central orchestrator that holds all your funnel knowledge is what turns a pile of files into a system anyone on the team can query instantly.
◆ The real unlock — most people get this wrong

The biggest problem isn't making the orchestrator "perfect." You can refine that forever. The real problem is instant access to every piece of knowledge in your funnel. When anyone on your team can ask "what's our offer for cold LinkedIn leads?" and get an answer in two seconds, that speed becomes a retention advantage. Knowledge you can reach beats knowledge you merely have.

Step 2 — Instrument Every Step, or the Second Half of Today Does Not Work

This is the part people skip, and it's the part that decides whether you have a funnel you can improve or a funnel you can only rebuild. Every step fires one event. The count of that event is the metric. A rate is one count divided by another.

#EventFires whenWhere the count comes from
1sessionthe entry page loadsAnalytics + your own event store
2startfirst interaction — first field, first question, first playAnalytics + event store
3qualify_completethe qualification questions are answeredAnalytics + event store
4step_answereach individual question or milestone — carries its own idEvent store + session recording
5engage_completethey finish the main body — the assessment, the session, Part 1Analytics + event store
6goals_completegoals and history capturedAnalytics + event store
7result_viewthe personalised result or offer reveal is shownAnalytics + event store
8offer_viewthe pricing or plan screen is shownAnalytics + event store
9checkout_startcheckout opensAnalytics + payment provider
10purchasethe charge succeeds — confirmed server-sidePayment API + CRM
11upsell_takean add-on is acceptedPayment API + CRM
Two destinations, always. Send every event to your analytics platform and to a first-party endpoint you control. Analytics gives you the exploration tools; your own store means you still have the data when a platform changes its API, its retention window, or its price.
◆ Pro tip · event number 4 is the one that pays for itself

Per-question and per-milestone drop-off is how you find out that question seven is costing you a fifth of your completions. Aggregate completion rate tells you something is wrong. Per-step drop-off tells you exactly what to delete.

Task 4.2Fire All Eleven, Then Prove They Arrive

Instrument, then verify — the verification is the task.

  1. Install analytics and a session-recording tool. Both have free tiers; there is no excuse.
  2. Fire every event to both destinations, with the UTM attached so buyers map back to a channel.
  3. Walk the funnel yourself, end to end, on a phone, and watch the events land in real time.
  4. Confirm each one is queryable through an API — not just visible in a dashboard. If an agent can't fetch it headlessly, your weekly loop will be manual forever.
OwnerYou · agent wires itToolAnalytics · recordings · your event endpointTime2–3 hDeliverable11 events live, queryable by APIProofOne real session produces all 11 in order

Step 3 — Wire the Pipeline

Events tell you what happened on a page. The pipeline tells you what happened to a person. You need both, and the pipeline is what makes forecasting possible.

Eleven stages, two exits, and the automation that guards each one

Step 4 — The Eight Automations

These are the eight a webinar needs (an RSP and a challenge shift the count; see below), and they carry the load. Each is a trigger, a condition and an action — and each one replaces a thing a human would otherwise forget to do.

Trigger → condition → action, eight times
Automations 1–6 are event-driven and fire instantly. 7 and 8 are polled, because inboxes and clocks don't send webhooks — and the polling interval is a cost decision, not a technical one.
Build them in this order. 1, 3 and 4 are the minimum viable set — confirm, capture, and tag. Everything else is leverage you add once the first three are provably reliable.
Task 4.3Wire the Pipeline and the First Three Automations

Don't try to build all eight today. Build the three that stop you losing data, and test each one with a real contact before moving on.

  • Custom fields first — source, UTM, the four tags, score and band. Adding a field later means back-filling every contact you've already captured.
  • Then the pipeline stages, with the trigger for each transition written down next to it. A stage with no trigger is a stage you'll be updating by hand.
  • Then automations 1, 3 and 4. Register yourself. Attend. Then register again and deliberately no-show. Confirm the tags land correctly both times.
OwnerYou · agent wires itToolYour CRM + automation toolTime4–6 hDeliverablePipeline + fields + 3 live automationsProofA deliberate no-show gets the no-show tag without you touching anything
◆ What changes per funnel type · the automations
Webinar FunnelAll eight apply as written. Automation 8 is the heaviest lifter — the timed reminder engine is what carries show-up to 89%.
Workshop · ChallengeAdd a ninth: the daily generation loop. Survey submitted → agent generates the day's output → PDF and link delivered. It runs once a day, three days running, and it is the product.
Reverse SqueezeAutomation 8 disappears entirely — there's no clock. It's replaced by depth-threshold triggers, which fire per person rather than per schedule.
Other types: tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels need a fulfilment trigger on purchase · product launches need a hard cart-close job that actually disables checkout · JV funnels need attribution and payout splitting at the moment of sale, because reconciling it later is how partnerships end.

Step 5 — Point Real Traffic at It

Everything up to now is a hypothesis. The only thing that turns it into knowledge is strangers. Today you run a deliberately small test — small enough that being wrong is cheap, big enough that the result isn't noise.

The test campaign — what to spend, what to watch, what it means
The point of today's traffic is not sales. It's to find out which of yesterday's assumptions was wrong, while being wrong is still cheap.
Task 4.4Run the Test and Write Down What Broke
  1. QA first. Every page at 375, 768 and 1280px. A real purchase. Every event firing. Do not send traffic to a funnel you haven't walked yourself.
  2. Launch the smallest version of each live channel, all UTM-tagged, all pointing at one URL.
  3. Wait. Reading numbers after four hours is how people kill things that were working.
  4. Pull both reports and find the single worst step. Not the worst three. The worst one.
  5. Write down what surprised you. That sentence is the most valuable output of the entire day.
OwnerYouToolYour channels + both reportsTime2 h to launch, then waitDeliverableLive traffic, both reports, one named bottleneckProofEvery buyer traces back to a channel via their UTM
◆ Your Day 3 output — half one

A live funnel at a real URL, built from a spec you can edit, with all eleven events firing to two destinations, a pipeline that updates itself, the three critical automations running, real traffic flowing through it, and both reports assembled — plus one named bottleneck to attack tomorrow.

◆ Tonight's homework · 20 minutes

Let the traffic run overnight. Don't touch anything. Tomorrow is about reading what it tells you and deciding what to change — and you cannot read a signal you keep interrupting.

Half two · grow it

Read the Numbers, Fix the Worst One, Repeat

You have a funnel and you have data. This half is the discipline that turns those into a business: know your unit economics, find the single worst step, change one thing, measure, keep or revert. Every week, forever.

◆ Why one leak at a time

Fixing five things at once feels productive and teaches you nothing — if the number moves you can't say which change did it, and if it drops you can't say which to undo. One change per leak is slower per week and vastly faster per quarter.

Step 1 — Know What a Customer Costs and What They're Worth

Two numbers decide whether you have a business or an expensive hobby: what it costs to acquire a customer, and what that customer is worth over their life. If the second is comfortably bigger than the first, you can buy growth. If it isn't, more traffic just loses money faster.

◆ Pro tip · the ratio, not the number

A $600 cost per customer is not "high" or "low" on its own. Against a $400 lifetime value it's a business that dies; against a $4,000 one it's a business you should be pouring money into. Watch the ratio. Roughly 3× is the conventional floor for a healthy funnel, and below about 1× you are paying for the privilege of having customers.

◆ Do this · replace every slider with your own fetched number

The sliders are for building intuition. The real version has your numbers in it, pulled from the reports you assembled yesterday — and any term you still can't fetch stays marked unknown until you instrument it. A model built on plausible-looking guesses is worse than no model, because you'll trust it.

Step 2 — Find the Leak, Then Fix the Right Thing

Compare every step rate to the rest of your funnel, and to itself last week. The lowest one — or the one that dropped — is where you work. Here's what each leak usually means and what to change.

Leak diagnosis — the symptom, the likely cause, the one thing to change
Note the difference between the last row and every other row: the first seven are funnel problems, the last is a traffic problem. Fixing the wrong category is the most common wasted week.

Step 3 — Run the Loop Every Week

Six steps, one lap per week, forever
The loop can run semi-autonomously: the agent fetches both reports on a schedule, flags the worst leak and proposes a variant — you still decide what ships.
And the bottleneck always moves. Fix the worst step and a different one becomes the worst. That's the loop working, and it's why this is a weekly habit, not a project with an end date.
Task 5.1Run One Full Lap Today
  1. Observe — pull both reports from yesterday's traffic.
  2. Locate — name the single worst step out loud. Write it down.
  3. Hypothesise — one sentence: "I think it leaks because ___, so I'll change ___."
  4. Experiment — put the variant in the spec, serve it to half your sessions, keep everything else identical.
  5. Diary it — the change, the date, the metric you expect to move, and what you'll do either way. Future you will not remember.
OwnerYou · agent fetchesToolBoth reports + your specTime60 minDeliverableOne live experiment + an experiment logProofBoth arms are being served and counted separately

Step 4 — Move the Money to the Channel That Actually Buys

Here's the rule that saves the most money: reallocate toward the lowest cost per buyer, not the lowest cost per click. A cheap click that never converts is the most expensive traffic you own.

Same spend, redistributed by cost per buyer
Figures are a teaching model. The method is not: rank by cost per buyer, fund the top, starve the bottom, keep a small test budget on everything so you'd notice if it changed.
◆ Pro tip · never cut a channel to zero

Leave a small always-on test budget everywhere. Channels change — an audience gets cheaper, a platform changes its algorithm, a competitor stops bidding. If you cut to zero you'll never find out, and you'll be the last to know when the cheapest channel in your market becomes available again.

Step 5 — The 52-Week Engine

Most of your list won't buy this month. The engine is what keeps them warm until the month they do — and what turns your existing customers into the cheapest traffic you'll ever get.

A year of contact, on four rails, from one topic rotation

Step 6 — Where $1M ARR Actually Comes From

Not from one enormous month. From a wheel that gets slightly easier to turn each time: a new customer joins, gets a fast win, asks for more, gets it, stays, and refers. Every turn adds recurring revenue and lowers the cost of the next customer.

The flywheel — customers never exit, they re-enter
AttractEngageDelightRevOps at the hub
LeverWhat you changeWhy it compounds
More buyersFix the worst funnel step; move budget to the lowest cost per buyerLinear — real, but it stops the moment you stop spending
Higher priceStrengthen the value equation until the price is obviously fairImmediate, and it flows into every calculation below
AscensionMake sure the rung above exists, and that buyers are told about itThe cheapest revenue you will ever earn — they've already bought
RetentionThe first 48 hours after purchase, and a fast first winMultiplies every number above it. This is the actual north star
ReferralAsk advocates directly, and make sharing trivially easyLowers acquisition cost, which raises the ratio, which funds more traffic
◆ Retention is the only lever that multiplies the others

Doubling your traffic doubles your buyers. Doubling your retention doubles the value of every buyer you have ever acquired and every one you will acquire. That's why the north star here is recurring revenue, not the first sale — and why the 48 hours after someone pays deserve more of your attention than the 48 days before.

Task 5.2Write the Scale Plan

One page, five lines. Then put the weekly review in your calendar as a recurring event, because a loop that isn't scheduled is a loop that runs twice and stops.

  1. My cost per buyer is ___ and my lifetime value is ___. Both fetched, neither guessed.
  2. My cheapest channel is ___, so next month's budget moves toward it.
  3. My worst step is ___ and this week's experiment is ___.
  4. My ascension offer is ___ — the rung above what they just bought.
  5. My retention mechanism is ___ — what produces the first win, and by when.
OwnerYouToolOne pageTime45 minDeliverableScale plan + a recurring weekly reviewProofLines 1 and 2 contain fetched numbers, not estimates
◆ What changes per funnel type · scaling
Webinar FunnelScale by frequency — run it monthly rather than occasionally. The assets are already built, so each additional run costs mostly promotion. Watch show-up rate as volume grows; it usually dips first.
Workshop · ChallengeScale by cohort size and cadence, but completion rate is the constraint. A cohort too large to feel personal converts worse on the last day — and the last day is where the money is.
Reverse SqueezeScale by content volume. Each new Part 1 is a permanent new entrance, and old ones keep producing. Slowest to start, best compounding of the three.
Other types: tripwire and free-plus-shipping funnels scale on ad spend, limited only by how fast the upsell recovers acquisition cost · community funnels scale on member-driven referral and stall if the community goes quiet · JV funnels scale by adding partners, so partner recruitment becomes the growth function.
◆ Your Day 3 output — half two

Your scale plan: unit economics you fetched rather than guessed, a channel budget ranked by cost per buyer, one live experiment on your worst step, the 52-week engine segmented and scheduled, and a standing weekly review in the calendar.
